My entire knowledge of Iceland in 4 minutes & 7 seconds After some furious research I created something vaguely resembling a plan, made a couple of bookings, was given a jumper, and figured if it all went horribly wrong at least my frozen corpse would be cryogenically preserved striking an awesome pose inside some Icelandic glacier. Hopefully long enough there’s been 3 or 4 alien invasions to really clear the place out before I’m revived First impression flying into Iceland was that it’s not… really… inviting… Unless you’re really into lifeless volcanic outcroppings Also turns out you don’t fly into Reykjavik: you fly into Keflavik, out on the Reykjanik peninsula about 50km away from Reykjavik. Which suited me just fine, as where I’d hired a campervan from was right near the airport and I’d had more than enough of seeing/hearing/smelling/tasting people over the last few months – avoiding the capital fitted well with my plan to escape humans for at least a few days. Picking up my “Happy Camper”, I decided to test out this whole “driving on the right-hand side of the road business” by driving around the local neighborhood to get the hang of having everything reversed. After driving the back streets (only going around a roundabout the wrong way once) I managed to grab camping food for the next 3 days from the local supermarket (using a combination of mime & animal noises to communicate with the cashier who spoke perfect English) and found an awesome Viking statue. My bird, beard & axe game are severely lacking here Emboldened by my Viking brethren, it was time to start the adventure and venture out onto the highway: I was on it 2 minutes before I stalled the camper trying to take an exit, stranding me halfway across a dual-carriageway on a blind corner. The camper refused to start, the car behind me started beeping, I threw on the hazard lights sending the car behind me into a blind honking-rage, before the engine eventually restarted on the 6th go and I pulled clear of an oncoming semi-trailer. Glad to say the driving for the rest of the trip was relatively uneventful… Rather than racing to all the usual tourist spots I wanted to get out and away from people (especially ones driving other vehicles). Hafnir was relatively close, on the coast, and sounded vaguely like the name of a battlemech in Mechwarrior (because I’m psychologically 7 years old). And as you’d expect from a place I randomly chose based on its tenuous link to a video game I played 15 years ago, there was nothing to see except the set of Biodome 2. Pauly Shore films don’t get the budgets they used to But just down the coast was a place where you could walk across a bridge connecting the North American & Eurasian continental plates… Shout out to my high school geography teacher who said “plate tectonics are just a theory”… just like gravity And another place called Gunnuhver, where the Icelandic believe a demonic ghost lives and geothermal steam jets out of the ground (these two things are probably connected). “Please don’t shove your face in the vent of stones producing super-heated steam that we named after a demon” Working my way around the peninsula, I found myself being followed by a pair of German tourists. This became a common theme during my time in Iceland whenever I was on any of the “ring” roads – the same people stopping to look at the same incredibly stunning scenery you stopped to look at, leaving after about the same amount of time it took you to get bored with it, before driving in the same direction and turning up to ruin your next stop with their peopleness. The Atlantic Ocean – largely untainted by peopleness We reached peak peopleness when I stopped at the Blue Lagoon. The Blue Lagoon itself held little to no appeal to me, but everyone raves about it being a “must visit” and it was on my way, so I figured I’d at least call in to see what all the fuss was about. And lo and behold, it’s a pale blue lagoon. Please hold your gasps of shock & astonishment It was also terrifyingly touristy. The whole place was setup like a hotel-resort, funneling everyone into a lobby and restaurant, charged access to swim in the lake, and you literally had to exit via gift shop. And every asshole in Iceland was there with their obnoxious screaming kids. I snapped a selfie as evidence I’d been there (above), used their marble toilets and bolted out of there. How’s the serenity? The whole point of spending a few days in a camper driving around Iceland was that I didn’t have to interact with people if I didn’t want to (I didn’t), and I could disconnect from the rest of the world to enjoy the natural beauty of Iceland. So I connected my SIM-less phone to the stereo, put the Martian soundtrack on loop, and followed the south coast. The camper hire guy had said I’d get around Iceland a lot quicker than I might expect, and he was dead right – I’d driven half the south coast before midday, and my only plan had been to drive that before heading to Thingvellir national park to camp overnight ready for my dive at Silfra the next morning. So with about 11 hours of sunlight left (welcome to the land of the midnight sun) I headed inland towards Geysir instead, where the word “geyser” comes from. The Icelandic are a very literal people With the icy wind blowing off the mountains, I decided to have my first meal in the camper – cracking the side door just enough not to gas myself on the stove fumes but without freezing either. It’s a delicate balance being this classy After another venture into a hyper-touristy hotel/resort at Geysir – to abuse a toilet, drain the dregs of my 2-minute noodle soup out in the car park, then leave again – I decided “national park” sounded like the place likely to have the lowest peopleness. Heading south-west into Thingvellir national park, you can see why they filmed Game of Thrones here. I think. I mean, I’ve never watched it and never plan to, but I know there’s a bunch of medieval families straight up murdering each other at an awesome wedding, and vague claims of dragons. Which all sounds like it should be filmed in the same place Vikings came from. It also probably explains why the show “Vikings” is filmed here. Which I’ve also never seen. Probably because I’m too busy visiting these places instead of watching shows filmed here There was still plenty of light when I parked at Silfra – where I’d be diving the next morning – so I decided to have a look around. Walking along a path through a schism in the sheer rock face, I turned around and saw this… All of the pretty … about 10 seconds before another tourist walked up to me and said “Excuse me, do you know which side is North America?”. Just like the bridge between two continents, Thingvellir national park is situated right where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates are pulling apart. I worked out we were facing North and told him “The mountains on the left”. All that smart ass geography knowledge didn’t mean a damn when it came to settle in for the night though – the guy who hired me the camper told me that “most campsites are open all year round” but do you think I could find one with an unlocked toilet and shower? After driving around the whole park I eventually found one that at least had the disable toilet unlocked, and seems like it was the only one in the region too because I had multiple people knock on my camper door around twilight asking if I’d seen any other sites with unlocked toilets and showers. So much for escaping peopleness. I’d be in for a little more peopleness the next morning, but it’d all be worth it though: I’d be taking the plunge at one of the top 10 dive sites in the world. While all of Thingvillir national park is formed by the North American & Eurasian tectonic plates pulling apart, Silfra is the spot in Thingvillir where water running off the mountains emerges after 75+ years of limestone filtering to form a freshwater lake. So besides the fact you’re diving between two continents, you’re also diving in the highest visibility water in the world (measured at over 120m/393ft), and it feels a bit like you’re spacewalking instead of diving. Camping just up the road meant I was there before all the divers driving from Reykjevik, so I chatted to our surface support instructor Tanya while she set the gear up & we waited. I was qualified as a TDI Advanced Trimix diver and instructing for both PADI & SSI prior to moving to the UK to join the Royal Marines, but I really haven’t been diving regularly since then. So while the knowledge & experience are all still there I was definitely rusty, and it was great having the team from DIVE.IS looking after us. The water at Silfra is also about 2°C, which meant wearing some incredibly sexy dry suits… Dry suit is borrowed but the sexy beanie is all mine. I was grouped up with Johnathon (an English uni student who’d just done his Open Water course in the Red Sea) and Pien (an Californian lady who was only on her 4th dive ever) to be led by our dive guide Rob who’d just finished a season instructing and leading dives through the WW1 German wrecks at Scarpa Flow (one of my all-time “places to dive before I die/go to Mars”). Our first dive was really just a check out so we could get used to the dry suits, but it was still extraordinary. Pien struggled with her buoyancy & ears, so Rob spent most of the dive looking after her. I kept a casual eye on Johnno at the same time, but he adapted to the dry suit really quickly so we spent most of the dive soaking up as much of the underwater scenery as we could. It was still bloody cold though, and after the first dive and a hot chocolate on the surface Pien was so cold she decided to skip the 2nd dive. Which is a shame because it’s when Rob, Johnno & I got the best pictures, like hanging onto two continents at once… North American plate in my left hand, Eurasia in my right … and diving on something that felt like a blue-tinged moonscape. You can check out the full gallery here, but it’s safe to say the experience was absolutely extraordinary. After swapping cards and hugging a huge thanks to everyone, it was off on the next adventure into the Icelandic highlands! In July 2015 Mars One’s CEO Bas Lansdorp was scouting locations for a mock Mars habitat, and posted photos & coordinates for two possible sites in Iceland – one near Vik, and the other in the highlands near Suðurland. So I figured if I was in the country and it was so easy to get around I’d check them out myself, starting with the Suðurland site. Welcome to the Icelandic Highlands Turns out driving around Iceland is really easy unless you want to drive on an “F-Road”. I can think of a few things the F stands for, but basically you’re not able – physically or legally – to drive on an F-Road unless you’re in something that is half 4WD & half monster truck. Do your wheels even lift bro? There’s no way my puny campervan was going to cut it, but sure enough as I pulled up at the sign marking the start of the F-road the camper’s Tom Tom was telling me the Mars One site was another 8km ahead. What the Tom Tom wasn’t telling me though was that I’d be slogging the whole way through about 2 feet of snow drift to get there. There’s no doubt it was cold when I started the hike, but it was less than 20 minutes before I was stripping out of my thermals down to a shirt & jeans. And hour & a half later I was walking around in circles trying to get a GPS lock on the coordinates Bas had shared… … before finally finding the right spot It’s difficult to describe just how desolate the whole area is. Besides some power lines way off to East that you really have to look for to see, there’s no sign of humanity or life generally. I’d kept my headphones in during the hike there, and was dumbfounded by how still & quiet the place was when turned the music off. As in eerily quiet – no wind, no birds, nothing. After snapping my photo in a place specifically selected for its barren emptiness, it was time to hike back to the camper. With everything covered in snow and no frame of reference I’d had a nightmare trying to navigate in, but using the power lines and the hill I’d climbed to get to the plateau as a heading the return journey was much quicker… and also lead me straight towards a cliff I’d skirted on the way in. After some improvised tobogganing (eg. holding my bag to my chest and sliding on my ass down 200m of snow drift) I managed to get back to the river just a kilometer from where I’d parked. The snow on the right is a LOT higher than it looks So after about 4 hours of hiking and without another soul for at least 10km, I figured a trip to Iceland wouldn’t be complete without a skinny dip in water that was flowing off highland glaciers. I could say this has been tastefully cropped, but the 2 degree water made overexposure less of an issue There was fair bit of light when I got back to the camper, so I figured I’d at least try to get to the other Mars One site at Vik too. Heading back down from the highlands and toward the southern coast both fuel and light were getting very low, but I still stopped to grab a photo of this little gem. The hotel of my people By the time I nursed the car into the service station at Vik and figured out the bizarre payment system for fuel it was well and truly twilight, and there was no way I’d be able to find the second Mars One site in the dark. I’d driven passed some amazing waterfalls and watched the sunset on Eyjafjallajökull (the volcano that shut down air traffic in Europe for 6 days in 2010) and Katla (Eyjafjallajökull’s much bigger sister), so I headed back towards the camping grounds I’d seen on the way to Vik – trying to find somewhere with very few lights in the vain hope of spotting the aurora. With total cloud cover the aurora was a no-show, but unbeknownst to me I wound up parking for the night with a waterfall directly behind me… … and one of Iceland’s most famous waterfalls a short walk away. Seljalandsfoss waterfall looking glorious And as you’d expect from one of Iceland’s most famous waterfalls, the place was packed with tourists. After a few photos of the waterfall (and dunking my head in a stream as a pseudo-shower) I scampered out of there pretty quick. But with the drive/hike in the highlands and a few nights to myself without wifi, I’d had something of a breather from peopleness. After a gorgeous drive to Selfoss through the southern mountains and skimming the edge of Reykjavik, it was time to drive back to Keflavik and return the camper. I stayed the night in a place about 9km from the airport, watching The Expanse till midnight & waiting for it to get dark enough to finally catch the aurora. But even with clear skies it never really got dark enough before the sun was coming back up again, so I guess I’ll just have to come back when the nights are longer! And probably stay in one of these bubbles for it The next day it was time to say goodbye to Iceland, so after a slow start & an awesome breakfast I figured I had plenty of time to skip the taxi and walk to the airport – popping the headphones back in and starting the hour & a half walk. I’d been warned by a friend who’s a huge Kim Kardashian fan (don’t worry, I judge her too) that Kim & Kanye were in Iceland at the same time, and low and behold just as I was walking passed the end of the runway I had their private jet take off right over my head. Personally I’m just really glad Yeezy didn’t decide to flush at the same time. Please don’t There’s been so much happening I’m about 3 weeks behind on these posts (currently in Washington D.C ahead of the Humans 2 Mars conference starting Tuesday). But the next step was flying into Boston for a few days before a weird weekend in NYC, and without going into details a lot has changed personally since I got through that. Spending 6 days being a complete space geek in Florida certainly helped too – the trip feels very much like it’s “mine” now. So I’m looking forward to getting those trip entries written & published in the next few days too 😀 - Dave Looking good mate - Josh Thanks Dad 🙂 - Mandi Ryan I’m really enjoying your posts Josh. Great to see what you are up to. Hope everything else goes well too! - Josh Cheers Mardi – there’s plenty more to follow! - Shelley Richards Is it weird if your Mum posts comments too? It is, isn’t it? Oh well, here goes: loved reading this one Josh and missing having regular contact with you but great to know that you are (again/still) exploring the big wide world. x - Josh Haha, more than OK Mum 😀 Great speaking to you both this today, and I’ll try to call a little more regularly than I have. ### Recent Posts - News – The best, the worst, & the breather [Florida] - News – Space museum overload & Mars One meetups [Washington D.C.] - News – Boston Buddies, Space Shuttles & Bottoming Out [Boston & NYC] - News – Diving between continents & hiking to desolation [Iceland] - News – Airport Hell, Involuntary Weight Loss, & UK Mars100 Meetup - News – Life in a Box, Festival Madness & Going Global - News – 2016 “Cosmic Nomad” Global Tour - News – The Martian Stunt #bringhimhome - SHSSP16 Week 3 – Fighting Flat Earthers, New Management & Cultured Chaos - SHSSP Week 2 – Goodbye Spaceman, Buzz Day & Payload Tension - SHSSP Week 1 – Droids, Starmen & Grabthar’s Hammer - News – That whole “Moving to the other side of the country” thing - News – Helena National Science Week Tour - Mars One – Parachuting & Media Mayhem - Mars Project – You Are Go To Continue Descent… - News – 2015: The Year Space Kicks It Up a Notch - Random – Fringe World for People Who Aren’t Old & Boring - Random – An Open Letter to Myself in 2020 - News – There and back again… (Part 2: Australia) - News – There and back again… Part 1: Europe
title: Website – Diving between continents & hiking to desolation Iceland

content:
While I was waiting to board my flight from Cape Town to Addis Ababa a few weeks back, a strange thing kept happening on the gate information screen: in clear white letters was “Addis Ababa” with the correct gate and boarding time, but every now and then “Addis Ababa” would change into “Gaborone” and go a dark yellow colour. All the other flight details matched up though, and I boarded the flight with no issues, so I just put it down to being an alternative name for Addis Ababa.
It wasn’t. It’s the capital of Botswana. They flew us to Botswana. Do you know where Botswana is Because I sure as hell didn’t til I landed there.
This looks… inviting?
Turns out we needed to stop and refuel to make the distance to Addis Ababa, but Ethiopian Airlines figured we didn’t really need to know this until we were taxiing to the runway. To be honest stopping for an hour to refuel wasn’t really an issue for most of the passengers, but it was a fairly major issue for me, because I sat on a window just behind the wing & had to watch the plane being refueled by the loosest man alive – hence forth known as “LMA”.
Picture this: The fuel truck drove up, LMA leaps out and places a rickety wooden ladder under the wing. He runs back, grabs a wire off a reel and connects it to the plane’s wing as an earth. Then he wanders back, grabs the fuel line, drags it over to the rickety wooden ladder, connects it to the wing, then wanders back to the tanker and turns the pump on.
All pretty standard stuff, except for the bit where LMA then sits next to the pump pushing hundreds of liters of jet fuel a minute and answers a couple of calls on his handheld radio, makes a couple of calls on his mobile, and then because he’s bored decides to have a smoke…
He’s facing away from us because cool guys don’t watch explosions
LMA managed to refuel the plane without incinerating himself or the ~150 people on-board, and we left to begin a whole new circus in Addis Ababa. The only person I know who’s spent any time in Ethiopia is an old girlfriend I’ve only just started speaking to again (honestly, 5 years almost felt too soon… but we’re okay now), so a few weeks before the flight I asked her if it was worth leaving the airport. She warned me that Bole International Airport was a “hellhole” and kindly organised for one of her old teaching buddies to pick me up and take me out for dinner….
…which would have been amazing if I hadn’t arrived to discover Ethiopian immigration only let people out of the airport if their stopover is more than 8 hours – mine was 7 & a half.
We’d arrived half an hour early (probably because of LMA’s efficient refueling), so after braving one of the toilets I rushed around trying to find wifi to message the ex’s friend and say I couldn’t get out of the airport. Turns out the “Free Wifi” at Bole International is only “free” if you know the wifi password… which you can only get if you pay one of the dodgy shop owners. So after paying $10US to use an internet cafe that wasn’t connected to the internet (“no refund!”), and another $10US to have a shop owner type the wifi password into my phone (“you no look at code!” as she grabbed my phone and turned away from me), I managed to get through the ex’s friend to say I wouldn’t be able to leave the airport, just as she was about to leave her house to pick me up.
I’d had a fairly big night fueled by nachos and margarita-slushies in Cape Town before I left, and there’d been next to nothing to drink on the flight, so with “Escape from Bole” aborted the next challenge was to try to find water. This would have been easy if I could drink what was leaking from the roof, but “Drink Ethiopian airport roof water” isn’t on my “101 Things To Do Before I Die” list.
This is just like the “Free Wifi”, except the buckets are advertised as “Shower Facilities”
I couldn’t even pay to use one of the Ethiopian Airline Lounges (“Are you business or first class Then no”) so after a futile search for water fountains I just curled up in a ball on one of lounges, clutching all my worldly possession to my chest for 6 hours and dreaming of bottled water.
Welcome to WHAT?
After some next-level Orwellian insanity at the boarding gate (3 x-ray luggage scans without leaving the security area of the airport) at 1am local time, I was back on my way to the UK. It’s not that I hated every second at Bole International Airport… it’s just that if I ever go there again in this lifetime it will be too soon.
Accurate photo of me flying out of Addis Ababa
Back on-board things were a little more sane – Ethiopian Airlines isn’t great, but atleast this flight the sound to my entertainment system worked (as opposed to my flight into Addis Ababa where I watched “Edge of Tomorrow” on mute) and there was water: I think I went through half a dozen of those little bottles of water before they cut me off.
I landed at Heathrow around 7:30am, walked straight off the plane to Customs & Immigration (joys of being a registered traveller with no checked luggage) was on the Heathrow Express by 8:00, Paddington station by 8:15, and walked into the Space Innovation Congress (SIC) in St Paul’s at just after 9:00. Because apparently I work on ISU time all the time now.
SIC wasn’t really aimed at me (more for space entrepreneurs trying to start commercial space ventures) but it was fantastic catching up with Dr Alice Gorman over from Adelaide to talk about cultural heritage in space, as well as finally meeting Professor Chris Welch (who run’s ISU’s Masters Program) after emailing & tweeting the last 2 years in since I finished SHSSP14. There were claims of Buzz Aldrin making an appearance that never materialised, and I knew there was an astronaut panel organised after lunch… but it was still a fantastic surprise to see Dr Bob Thirsk again! I’d only met Bob in January at SHSSP16, but that already feels like a lifetime ago.
I’ve been operating my phone without a SIM card since I left Australia (carrier doesn’t allow roaming), so anywhere with wifi has become an oasis in a communications desert. The conference had solid wifi, so I ducked out of the presentations a little early to place a couple of VoIP calls to my boss for SSP16 and some TV folks who want to talk science & comedy when I get to LA in mid-June.
Didn’t have long to chat though, because I needed to get out to Luton airport to meet an ex-girlfriend (Eli) who was flying in from Amsterdam. So I jumped on the nearest tube and bolted out to Luton… to discover you can’t use an Oyster card out to Luton – you have to buy a separate ticket. Just as well there were two inspectors waiting by the gate to issue fines, because it’s almost as if this is something that people do accidentally all the time…
After waiting for Eli at Luton (still no wifi, but atleast the roof wasn’t leaking like Bole International) we headed back into London… when I realised in amongst fighting train ticket inspectors and picking up an ex from the airport, I’d missed one of the most historic moments in the modern space age…
I’m retroactively making this the reason we broke up
With all the chaos going on I’d completely blanked on the fact that SpaceX were launching CRS8. But even if had remembered, there’s no way I could have watched it travelling through the wifi desert of Luton bus/train transfers. Still, mucho disappointo.
After a night in a dingy hostel in London (because I’d somehow forgotten just how generally awful London hostels are) we met up with old comedy friends Robbotron & Jo Jo Bellini for breakfast, then Eli & I headed down to Brighton with Megan – who’s garage I was living in when I found out about Mars One. First stop The best Mexican in the known universe…
Burrito fun times at La Choza with Eli & Meg
By the time we got home I was reaching burn out – the reality is I hadn’t truly stopped in the 3 months since SHSSP16 started, I’ve been carrying the ghost of a throat infection for the last 2 months, and emotionally really just needed to not see or speak to anyone for a solid few days. We struck a compromise by staying in so I could curl up on the couch, I introduced Eli & Meg to Rick & Morty, and Meg went and picked up fish & chips from down the road for dinner. Eli & Meg stayed up drinking wine and chatting, while I passed out on the couch in the lounge.
No no – just leave me here
At about 3am something stirred me, but I just lay there being angry at the world for disturbing my slumber – I found out the next morning someone was killed 50m down the road around that time, when a bar fight spilled out into the road and in front of a truck. But to be honest that was the last thing on my mind, because as I rolled over to go back to sleep my stomach suddenly turned… then turned again… and about 12 seconds later I was diving for a sink as the fish and chips made a surprise return to the world.
Food poisoning is a barrel of laughs if you’ve ever had it – fantastic way to lose weight. After hurling my body weight up, I managed to sleep through till about midday and also managed to pull off “being a pathetic mess” for the rest of the day too. So while Eli & Meg embraced the pancake love, I sipped on a flat coke. We ended up staying in again and I only started to get part of my appetite back nibbling on a pizza and watching the LEGO movie.
After the great purging of April 9th, atleast I woke up the next morning not wanting to die. Eli & I headed back to London, she flew back out to Amsterdam (after a weekend for us to catch up where I’d spent 3/4 of the time being a tragic, miserable asshole) and I headed out to dinner with a friend and to see the UK premiere of “Last Man On the Moon”.
Eugene Cernan – Gemini 9 pilot, Apollo 10 Lunar Module Pilot, and Apollo 17 commander – was literally the last person to stand on the Moon, and “Last Man On The Moon” is a documentary based on Cernan’s autobiography that’s been getting a lot of traction in the US. Cernan had been supposed to conduct a Q&A after the documentary screening, but health issues prevented him making the flight to London for the UK premiere.
The documentary was… I don’t know. It’s hard to be disappointed with a documentary about the last human to have walked on another world. But I really struggled, and the non-space friend who came with me was less than polite about it. There were some truly memorable & emotional parts (the interview with Roger Chaffee’s widow about the Apollo 1 fire comes to mind) and I’d still recommend people see it, but by the time we got to Cernan going to the Moon with Apollo 17 I was… bored. And to be honest it felt like it kind of ruined the otherwise great night I had with an old friend.
The next night in London was definitely an improvement though, because I was getting to meet 3 more of the Mars 100 had come all the way down from Durham, with Ryan MacDonald joining us from Cambridge and Clare Weedon too.
L-R: Ryan, some ginger skinhead, Hannah, Clare
It was incredible meeting Hannah, Clare & Ryan – besides it being a great get-together of folks all dedicated to the human colonisation of Mars, it’s also been fascinating seeing how my preconceived ideas about different candidates (gleaned from watching & reading their interviews) marry up with what they’re actually like in person. I’m sure given how many ridiculous interviews I’ve done over the last few years I’m sure many of the Mars 100 have a fairly skewed image of what I’m like, but on a selfish note it’s been really interesting to have those some of my preconceptions of the others challenged (and some confirmed) by meeting in person. I’m really grateful for the flexibility in this trip to meet as many of them as I can.
London town grows pretty old if you’ve lived their before though, so the next day it was time to head out to Bristol. It’s clearly been awhile since I took a train around the UK, because this one had on-board wifi all fancy like, and apparently it’s standard on a lot of the lines now. Getting into Bristol I had enough time to walk from the station to the hostel, drop my bags at the hostel in town, then walk back to the station and head back to Bath for dinner with some old friends from my time working for Damien Hirst! 100% worth it though – Vicky has always been my pseudo-sister in the UK, her boyfriend Olly is a fantastic guy, and the three of us had a lot to catch up on. The take home line for the night came from Vicky: “Josh, next time you’re planning on changing your whole life for some woman, just call me – I’ll tell you not to”.
I never listen though…
There were a half dozen people I could have caught up with in Bristol, but given I’d been bed-ridden by food poisoning a few days earlier I figured a rest day might be in order (sorry Ollie & Roxie). I managed to catch up with one other friend from Damien Hirst – Hugh, our carpenter who was one of the guys I worked closest with – but otherwise most of the day was spent trying to find a decent place for breakfast, writing, and booking accommodation for the rest of the trip.
As you’ve probably figured by now, there’s a fairly serious mis-match at the moment between my instagram feed (which shows where I am in the world at the same time I’m there) and these posts (this one’s about a week behind). Doing things is great, but catching up with people has certainly taken it out of me the last few months. Atleast the “bat shit crazy” time schedule has eased to “hectic” now though, so I’m starting to catch up.
Next stop was Dublin to catch up with good friend, science-communicator extraordinaire and ISU-buddy Niamh Shaw and her hilarious partner Peter (he ought to be funny, the man’s been a comedian/MC forever). There wasn’t much time to chat to Niamh & Peter though, because the mighty Barry was driving from Derry to pick me up for so we could wreak havoc on Cork for the weekend!
Two of Cleo’s 2016 Most Eligible Bachelors
We had grand intentions for our Saturday night in Cork, but the reality is after the best pizzas in the region at the Franciscan Well Barry and I kind of stumbled around a bit like lost sheep. We ended up befriending a couple of German girls who looked interesting but equally lost, found our way to Crane Lane (which I remembered from my last visit), mingled about, and then just kind of bailed: everywhere was wall-to-wall with people, and against our initial hopes of a big night I don’t think Barry or I were really feeling it.
Cork is also home to ISU’s 2017 Summer Space Program too, so Barry and I went and caused mischief for a morning at Blackrock Castle – which is playing a major role in SSP17 with it’s observatory and space science outreach program.
And spotted Niamh’s “To Space” show poster behind the front desk!
After Blackrock the only things left were to meet up for a coffee with another friend (which I may write about separately some other time), and drive back to Dublin! I waved goodbye to the mighty Barry from Niamh’s place, and spent the next few days trying to get my life in order by booking more flights, catching up on sleep, and getting some much missed running in – if I don’t get to stretch my legs every few days I get… weird.
Before you ask, yes – weirder than usual
Besides having some incredible evening chats with Niamh about her SSP15 experience which will directly affect the way I operate as a Teaching Associate on SSP16 in Haifa; the only thing of serious note from my days in Dublin was meeting Joseph Roche. Joe is a former Mars One candidate who earned a certain notoriety in early 2015 when he was quoted in a series of highly critical articles written by a journalist I know quite well. As an assistant professor in STEM education at Dublin’s Trinity College though, I’d wanted to meet Joe well before “Rochegate” (as it became known), and have always questioned how much was said “by Joe” was actually him, and how much was the journalist twisting what he was saying to suit her very clear agenda against Mars One (and space exploration generally).
I’d read Joe’s article in the Guardian which seemed to carry a much more reasonable message, but again it was important to meet him in person to get the real story. And the reality is he’s an absolute gentleman, a huge proponent of exploring and colonising Mars, but as time went on he decided Mars One didn’t have what it takes to succeed – and that is entirely okay. Where it all went wrong for him was expressing that to a journalist who had zero qualms twisting what he was saying into articles with titles like “Mars One Finalist Explains Exactly How It’s Ripping Off It’s Supporters” (I’m not linking it – look it up yourself if you must).
So really, the only one who “won” out of the entire episode was the journalist, and she’s not worth saying anything about anymore…
…but Joseph Roche is a great guy, and deserved to be treated a lot better by the world’s media than he was.
Overall though, it was great being able to stop for a good few days somewhere safe to rest properly (thank you so much again Niamh & Peter for welcoming me into your home) and time/headspace to plan the rest of my travels… including a last minute detour to Iceland that I’ll write about in the next post 😉
title: Website - Airport Hell

content: I have no idea where to even begin describing the roller-coaster my last 5 months have been, so let’s start with the basics. I Moved to Melbourne Yup, up and left. No real warning – just gone. Leaving Perth had been in the works since the start of 2015, and given I’d been visiting Melbourne at least once a month since November it made sense it’d be where I wound up… but I sure as hell wasn’t expecting it to happen so fast. The plan had been to visit Tasmania for a holiday in late April, return to Perth to close out a few things and say goodbye, then leave on May 31st – the day before the Sunday Times named me in their list “75 People who make WA great”. Instead what happened was: - Mid April I off-handedly applied for a job in Melbourne as a school lab technician, - The school interviewed me via Skype 5 days later, - They gave me the job an hour after the interview, - I flew to Tasmania for 3 days, - Then flew from Hobart to Melbourne and started work at the school the next day The whole thing – from applying to starting work – took less than 2 weeks. With that rush I wasn’t fully prepared for when I got here, so for the first month I was commuting 2 hours a day to get to a job I’d initially thought was a part-time, but was actually full-time – 8 hours a day, 5 days a week. Needless to say it was one hell of an adjustment. As with everything though, once you’re over the initial shock and start to figure things out, you adapt and problem-solve. Learning Melbourne’s public transport system, buying a bike, and moving into an amazing share-house in Carlton solved the commuting issues – 10 minute bike ride to one school campus, and a 10 minutes walk to the other. Convenience, bitches I switched to part-time work My lab tech job was a lifesaver initially – it got me out of Perth, used my degree and chemistry knowledge, and paid far more than I’d been paid by any job since I left the mining industry. But the plan had always been to work part-time – just enough to pay the bills so I could focus my time and energy on writing & speaking about space. That is what I’d wanted to move to Melbourne for. So while my job was pretty easy – I had far too much free time – and ticked a lot of boxes, being full-time wasn’t really letting me do what I’d moved here to do. It also added evidence to the idea I’m a cartoon character… After a visit to the Victorian Space Science Education Centre (VSSEC) and bumping into a friend in science communication, I decided I’d prefer the uncertainty of casual science communication work than keep going in a secure job that stopped me from doing all the cool stuff I really wanted to do. Rather than leaving immediately and leaving the school in a lurch, I told the school I’d stay the 6 weeks till the end of Term 3 – that way they had plenty of time to find a replacement for the start of Term 4 & I had a regular pay-check while I found something more suitable. The school started planning for my departure, and I started looking for a casual science job in between working and organising everything for National Science Week … until a week later when the principal struck on the genius idea of having me go part-time. It’s a great job, but it doesn’t need someone full-time – the reality is I was bored and frustrated that I had to be there 5 days a week. So now I’m on 3.5 days a week I’ve got the part-time job I was after, I’ve reclaimed the time & energy I needed to write (hence why you’re reading this), and the school has an enthusiastic lab technician who’s excited to be there rather than wishing he was doing something else. It also means I can keep riding to work four mornings a week: one hand on the handlebars, the other casually holding a soy latte like a job-less hipster. But of course right when all this job mischief was being discussed, I was also preparing for National Science Week… Helena Payload’s National Science Week Tour In case you missed it here, here, here, or any one of the dozen other places it was covered by the global media, I helped UWA’s Motorsport Team develop a payload for Mars One’s University Competition this time last year. What you might not know (because I never mentioned it until the previous post) is that the fine folks at Inspiring Australia gave us $15,000 to travel around the country during National Science Week to speak about Helena’s development and the experience of working on an aerospace engineering project. So Andre Van Vulpen, Rowan Heinrich, Claire Quy, and I bundled off for a flash tour of the country – taking in Perth, Hobart, Adelaide, Sydney and Melbourne. Speaking about Mars One at Hobart’s Festival of Bright Ideas Slipping away from the festival to visit Mt Wellington The Helena Team together at the University of South Australia In Adelaide, setting up our first presentation In Sydney to speak at OrbitOz Speaking at Uni High in Melbourne Speaking at Simonds Catholic College in Melbourne The Helena Team after our last presentation Speaking about Mars One at Monash University The chaos didn’t stop for me there though – while the rest of the team was flying back to Perth, I was running my “How To Become An Astronaut” workshop at Laneway Learning’s Science Spectacular, and the next evening I was presenting on the International Space University’s Southern Hemisphere Summer Space Program at RMIT’s Aerospace Industry Night. And somewhere in there I turned 30 too. Becoming Adult(ish) and doing Adult(ish) things Apparently 30 is some sort of arbitrary figure where ordinary people grow up emotionally, settle into a safe and secure job, get married, have 2.4 kids, and start the slow descent into death by mediocrity. But because I’m awesome and intend to die on a different planet to the one I was born on, I turned 30 and got a tattoo of a 7-leaf clover; 100 points if you get why this is about Mars … and because I’m wildly irresponsible I had a robot spaceman tattooed on my right ass cheek at the same time; By this point you might suspect I watch a lot of Futurama. You would be correct. Turning my life back into one long punch-line In July Mars One announced that the final astronaut selection phase will take place in September 2016. The candidates knew there were two possible selection periods (March or September 2016), and after being on this roller-coaster for nearly 3 years already a big part of me was hoping they’d go with March. But instead of being frustrated by another 6 months, I’ve realised I’ve got another 6 months to do all the stupid shit I want to do from the 101 Things list and write/tour a new comedy show about it. So now the race is on: since July I’ve attended a film premiere (#44), gotten a tattoo (#75), and I’m still chipping away at the greatest books list (#52). This whole website is due for some serious renovation, and updating the 101 Things list is the first thing to be updated. It’ll continue to be updated too as I do more stupid shit from the list when I return to full-time comedy next year. I’m currently writing my next science-comedy show “Cosmic Nomad”, so I’ll leaving my lab tech job (properly this time) at the end of 2015 to perform the show throughout 2016 – touring all the way around this shiny blue-green ball we call Earth until the final selection phase in September. The details of the tour are are still being worked out, but I’ll share them here as soon as everything is confirmed. In the meantime keep an eye out as I start to publish chapters from “Becoming Martian”; the book I wrote last year on how humans will change in physically, psychologically and culturally by colonising Mars. After sitting on the manuscript for 12 months I’ve decided I’d rather it be available for free online, rather than have it remain unread on my hard drive waiting for a publisher to wave a magic wand over it. And who knows – maybe I’ll collect all the posts together and sell it as a book during the 2016 Cosmic Nomad Tour… ### Recent Posts - News – Boston Buddies, Space Shuttles & Bottoming Out [Boston & NYC] - News – Diving between continents & hiking to desolation [Iceland] - News – Airport Hell, Involuntary Weight Loss, & UK Mars100 Meetup - News – Life in a Box, Festival Madness & Going Global - News – 2016 “Cosmic Nomad” Global Tour - News – The Martian Stunt #bringhimhome - SHSSP16 Week 3 – Fighting Flat Earthers, New Management & Cultured Chaos - SHSSP Week 2 – Goodbye Spaceman, Buzz Day & Payload Tension - SHSSP Week 1 – Droids, Starmen & Grabthar’s Hammer - News – That whole “Moving to the other side of the country” thing - News – Helena National Science Week Tour - Mars One – Parachuting & Media Mayhem - Mars Project – You Are Go To Continue Descent… - News – 2015: The Year Space Kicks It Up a Notch - Random – Fringe World for People Who Aren’t Old & Boring - Random – An Open Letter to Myself in 2020 - News – There and back again… (Part 2: Australia) - News – There and back again… Part 1: Europe - News – NatSciWeek Wrap Up & Roll on Europe - Mars Project – Becoming Martian & Other Science Week Madness

content:
7 Step Parachute Landing Fall
One of the first things you’re taught when you learn to parachute is how to land without breaking a leg. If you’re learning to free fall like I did, you’re eventually taught to pull down on the control handles and “flare” your parachute at just the right height for a smooth and soft landing. But the first landing you’re taught – and the only one you can use if something goes wrong or you’re using a round parachute – is a “PLF”, or Parachute Landing Fall.
Regardless of what others might say, a PLF still hurts… it just hurts less than trying to stay on your feet when you can’t slow down a landing. I’ve only ever had to do one: the free fall went fine, but when my parachute deployed I realised the wind was suddenly blowing at 20 knots in 180 degrees opposite to what it was when I jumped out of the plane. 180 degrees and 20 knots opposite what the jump was planned for.
I knew my parachute tracked forward at 15 knots in still air, but I was flying backwards. So I now had to choose between:
A) Turning with the wind to weave among trees before hitting the ground at 35 knots (~65km/hr) B) Turning against the wind to PLF into a hill before the trees, but hitting the ground backwards at 5 knots (~9km/hr)
I chose B: performing a PLF but still slamming backwards into a hill just meters short of the trees, and 8km off where I was supposed to land. I came home with a sprained ankle and a story – choosing A could have saved my ankle or killed me.
My point is that no matter how much you prepare and plan ahead for a major event, the unexpected can and often will happen. All you can do is take a deep breath, look at the problem in front of you, and use all you know as you do your damnedest to solve it and get out alive. Once you’re through the initial impact, you bundle up your parachute, say a quick thank you to the sky and the people who trained you, then you start limping home – a little wiser than you were before.
Over the last two years I’ve been slowly building up a network of journalists, educators and science communicators to update on Mars One’s progress. It’s why I left doing stand-up in the UK and moved back to Australia – I knew I could do more as an Australian in Australia than I could as an Australian in the UK. I’ve reached out to anyone I thought would be interested all across the world, and while I’ve had fun playing a role in raising awareness about Mars One the media interest hasn’t been overwhelming.
What I didn’t expect though was the sudden jump in interest that came with being selected into the final 100 astronaut candidates two weeks ago. I sent out a press release at 2pm WAST on Monday February 16th to ~30 people, expecting replies over a few days from the usual 4 or 5. Instead I did 8 radio and TV interviews in less than 2 hours. The next day there was another 16 interviews for radio, TV and newspapers. The same again the day after. As the news broke journalists shared my details amongst each other, and the whole thing started to snowball.
I’m still catching up on messages, and genuinely lost track of how much press I’ve done – at its peak I was doing 2 to 3 phone interviews via speaker phone while driving to a studio for another run of interviews. But here are a few of the highlights:
WA Today – Mars One: red planet a step closer for Perth man into top 100 (Feb 16) Triple J Hack – A Guy From Perth Could Be Going To Mars (Feb 16) SBS’s The Feed – The Mars One Mission: will it ever launch (Feb 16) News.com.au – WA comedian Josh Richards makes shortlist for Dutch space project Mars One (Feb 16) Channel 7’s Sunrise – Interview with Aussies waiting for Mars trip (Feb 17) Channel 9’s Today Perth News – Mission To Mars (Feb 17) RTRFM – Going To Mars (Feb 17) The Australian – Mars One mission: The seven Australians bidding for a one-way ticket (Feb 17) The Guardian UK – Mars One shortlist: the top 10 hopefuls (Feb 17) CNN – Round Two: 100 vie for one-way trip to Mars (Feb 18) That’s not even including the Today Tonight interview (can’t find the link) or the plethora of other radio interviews that happened: most assumed I lived in Melbourne or Sydney instead of Perth, so I was getting phone calls from east coast breakfast radio stations at 3am each morning saying “Sorry to call you at 6am”. It was unexpected, relentless and draining… but certainly nothing in comparison to surviving the sleep deprivation of a 5 day exercise with the Royal Marines, only to then be forced-marched through the night where I was hallucinating fences/training staff/oncoming trucks that weren’t there.
Or any other point in my time at Lympstone Commando. Like I said – you bundle up your kit, say thank you, and keep moving.
It was a welcome relief when the initial media rush slowed down on Wednesday afternoon though. I had a chance to embrace the end of the Perth fringe festival, support some incredible local comedian friends, see other amazing inter-state and international comedian friends, and finally retire Keith the Anger Management Koala with two incredible guest spots for “Mac the Comedy Computer” and “Tomás Ford is the End of the Fringe”.
That’s right: Keith the Anger Management Koala is dead.
Thankfully, thankfully dead
Many of the people interviewing me asked if “being in the Mars 100 has made the mission feel more real?”. The selection really didn’t change anything about the way I see Mars One, but finishing my final performance in a furry grey koala suit did. Everything I’ve done for the last two years (and everything I continue to do) has been shaped towards helping put humans on another planet. Keith was a shield so I could share stories from the military that were still too raw to share as myself – I shared those stories on stage at the Edinburgh Fringe in 2012, and the wounds were healed. I’ve wanted to retire Keith ever since, but it wasn’t until a few months ago I made the decision to let go of the suit completely – the Mars 100 announcement just before the end of the fringe was the perfect catalyst to make that happen.
That felt like I’d finally closed the book on something – letting me move forward without needing to glance back. So if you want more of the koala, the suit will be available to buy in a few months when I start fundraising for my flight to Mars One’s final selection phase. I’m not ever putting it on again, but I might dry clean it if you want it.
To seal in the decision, I slipped away to Margaret River for 3 days last week. Besides seeing some incredible sunsets,
and exploring some gorgeous caves…
…I had a chance to think about my past, present and future, and discuss it honestly with someone I love and trust. The Mars 100 announcement has been important, but in the grand scheme it’s just a fork in the road – if I hadn’t been selected to progress to Round 3 I’d still be trying to inspire people through space exploration, and would be in the process of shifting into building spaceships instead of training to fly them.
That may still happen in the future, but for now I’ll keep flying the flag as an astronaut candidate for Mars One. Especially when it gives me a chance to talk about colonising other planets to a crowd of astronomy fans gathered to break the Guinness World Record for “Largest Astronomy Lesson” in Kalamunda on Saturday night.
The previous record was ~830 people, we had over 1100.
And yes – the lights were turned off for the actual lesson…
I have no idea what comes next. But I’ve packed up my parachute, I’m eternally grateful for the incredible and continued support through this, and we’re already moving toward the final round of selection in the second half of this year – let’s see what the rest of 2015 brings.
title: Website - Parachuting & Media Mayhem

content:
The last two and a half years have been pretty odd.
In September 2012 I started researching how to send people one-way to Mars for a comedy show, and found an organisation aiming to do it for real. In 2013 I was one of 202,586 people who applied to be on the first crew to go, and one of 1058 short-listed for it. In 2014 I was one of 705 that passed the medical selection, and one of 660 offered an interview.
Today, I’m one of 100 people worldwide progressing to Mars One’s third round of astronaut selection.
Today I can tell you I had my selection interview in early December, and that I’ve waited to tell you about it for the last two and a half months because of a non-disclosure agreement with Mars One. And today I can finally tell you the knot that’s been sitting in my stomach for the last two weeks started to unwrap on Friday when I found out I’d made it through, that it’s unwrapping a little further sharing this with you now… but that it won’t fully clear until this all really sinks in Wednesday morning.
This afternoon I’ll be speaking to:
2UE in Sydney minutes after this is published (14:07 in Perth, 17:07 in Sydney), 6PR in Perth at 14:35 Perth Time Michael Smyth on Drive with ABC 891 Adelaide at 15:05 Perth time (17:35 in Adelaide), Barry Nicholls on Drive with ABC Regional (WA) 20 minutes later (15:15), Going national with Triple J’s Hack at 17:45. Tuesday morning I’ll be Channel 7’s Sunrise, and RTRFM’s Breakfast with Caitlin shortly after that. With the embargo lifted expect to hear a lot more of Mars One in the media this week. All 100 remaining candidates are expected to undergo group testing (likely in the US or Europe) before Mars One selects 24 to 40 of us to start full-time training in June/July. But right now I don’t know much about what the next few months will involve.
I’m grateful to have so many incredible people believe in what we’re doing – so many incredible people who believe in me. Some of you I’ve known for years, some I’ve really only just met. But all of you are vital to this journey – thank you so much.
I don’t know what happens next… but I’m really glad you’re here.
title: Website - Go to Continue Descent

content:
Let’s be honest here – a lot of people are really quite dull. They work, they eat, they sleep. Occasionally they watch A Current Affair to feel real emotions about how much they’re spending on dish-washing liquid, or if their 3 bedroom home in Ellenbrooke will be safe from ISIS.
Which is a shame, because life can be pretty amazing if you get off your ass, try new things, and stop being so damn scared of making mistakes. Some of you may already think you’re making a mistake reading this – this is entirely possible. “Hey, the title said something about Fringe World – I wonder if he’s got some show suggesti…”
Shut your face, I’m having a moment here.
There’s been a bunch guides recommending different Fringe World shows this last week, and almost all of them have recommended shows that have already sold out or will do soon. Don’t go to them. I’m not saying they’re bad shows – many of them are very, very good. But they don’t need you to see them – they’ve already got plenty of people who follow safe recommendations going, because “Hey, why would you want to see what might be the next big thing, when you can play it safe and see the current big thing?”.
Fringe festivals are supposed to be a chance for the less conventional, the less well-known, and frankly the flat-out weird performers out there to showcase what they do though. It’s not about loading up on more of the same safe crap you already know: “Oooooh, let’s go see him! I loved his TV special on Channel…”.
Seriously, I’m going to ask you to stop reading this if you keep interrupting with your beige-coloured, vanilla-flavoured opinions.
As I spent four years at the Edinburgh fringe and used to regularly dress up as a ukulele-playing koala that screamed at people for a living, I think I’ve got the authority to tell you what is “fringe” and what isn’t. Almost certainly more authority than anyone from the Sunday Times. If anyone from the Sunday Times would like to question that, please get in touch so I can arrange a meeting for you with my alter-ego Keith The Anger Management Koala, and he can politely inform you as to why you’re wrong.
And also explain why Christmas has been cancelled
The Fringe World UV Rating is reasonably accurate for finding weirdness, but there are some VERY notable exceptions. So I’m also going to give you a list of amazing shows to see to avoid being that boring wanker who turns up on Monday morning to work telling everyone he “saw Will & Woody doing stand-up“. Because while they’re nice guys, YOU CAN LISTEN TO THEM EVERY DAMN WEEKDAY MORNING FROM 6.
I’m seeing a lot of shows, but this is the proper fringe stuff I’m going to and you should too. Feel free to push your comfort zone at…
A Young Man Dressed As A Gorilla Dressed As An Old Man Sits In A Rocking Chair For Fifty-Six Minutes And Then Leaves. (Jan 29 – ONE NIGHT ONLY)
This is exactly what it says on the tin. It is also the ULTIMATE fringe experience. It’s so fringe it’s not even listed in the Fringe World guide, nor is it on their website. I saw “A Young Man…” in Edinburgh 2011, and it remains hands down the absolute best show I have ever seen at any festival anywhere in the world. It’s free, and I’ll be rocking up two hours early to make sure I can get in.
I say this without irony, or as part of any kind of trick: Please. For the love of God. See this show.
Mac The Comedy Computer’s Variety 52-Minute Spectacular! (Jan 24-Feb 21)
Ever watched a MacBook sit inanimate on a stage for nearly an hour, while the pre-recorded electronic voice of a sociopath plays over the sound system It’s hilarious and haunting. Mac is doing his first full fringe show, being joined on stage by Steve the Horribly un-PC PC as well as a variety of the weirdest and most confronting performers at Fringe World. This will probably destroy you.
Dr. Professor Neal Portenza performs his own autopsy live on stage. One night only. (Obviously). (Jan 28-Feb 12)
Whatever lunatic gave this a Fringe World UV Rating of “Medium” clearly didn’t even read the show title, let alone see the show. This show IS also running over multiple nights, because Neal Portenza is a mad man who clearly needs to be stopped.
Roaring Accordion (Feb 11-20)
Mimes cause a rather primal desire for violence to well up inside me, almost as much accordions do. That I’m still keen to see this should be an indication of how highly recommended the show is. I will however remain both skeptical and possibly armed.
Sarah Young’s Magical Murdery Mystery Tour (Feb 11-14)
Sarah Young is a ball of borderline-psychotic energy both on and off stage, who just won the Blue Room’s 2014 Judge’s Award for Best Writing for her play “Giving Up The Ghosts” where two people eat McDonald’s and then kill themselves. She also knows way to much about Big Foot, and will argue he’s real until she has an aneurysm. This show is not about sasquatch – it’s a whimsical show about serial killers. With hand puppets.
Pro-Choyce (Feb 18-21)
This is the full-size poster of Sian Choyce’s first solo show “Pro-Choyce”. Before you go to her show about how much she hates kids (I’ll be in the front row on opening night), you should click the image above and have a really good look her poster. Zoom in and read it. Look that – it’s an excellent poster. It’s also a poster you’re unlikely to see on walls anywhere at the festival, because Fringe World enlarged Sian’s A6 flyer to poster size and distributed THAT all over town instead.
Because it wouldn’t be a true fringe experience unless hard-working and talented performers were overcharged for incompetence.
Jeff Hewitt: V For Vagina (Feb 18-21)
I like Jeff. He’s a fun guy, and undoubtedly one of the best stand-up comedians in Perth. But he was also the kind of comedian that I’d never take a girlfriend to see unless I was trying to break up with her. Until now. From the trial material I’ve seen and the article Jeff recently wrote on why he’s doing a show about women called “V For Vagina”, I’m willing to take the risk.
But Jeff I swear to God, if I bring a date to this and afterwards she never wants to have sex for the rest of her life, you’re coming off the Christmas card list.
BRUCE (Feb 13 & Feb 14)
Bruce is a puppet made from a hacked apart block of foam, and needs two guys to make him talk. Those two guys however happen to be two of the most talented puppeteers in the world, and Bruce is one of the weirdest/funniest things you’ll ever see. Sammy J and Randy are great, but with my artist pass this is one of the only shows I’ll be paying to make sure I can see.
BLUES AND BURLESQUE:HOTTER THAN HELL (Jan 29-Feb 15)
I genuinely don’t get burlesque. Someone took me to see Dita Von Teese and her burlesque showcase in Seattle, and while it was great… I still didn’t get it. The women who do burlesque are unfailingly incredible, but the sexiness is usually all a little too serious for me. So unless it’s something hilariously warped – like a woman awkwardly trying to get out of a bee keeper’s outfit on stage – I’ll usually try to miss it. Maybe I’m just wired wrong.
There’s no sexy, angry bees in Vicious and Scarlett’s show, but they do have a hysterically warped sense of humour however, and Pete Saunders is absolutely exceptional providing the bluesy accompaniment.
If you enjoy regular burlesque shows, then Things That Go Bump…and Grind in the Night is definitely the place to be – all of the most entertaining burlesque dancers I know will be on, if they’re not actually behind the scenes running it.
Tomás Ford Is The End Of The Fringe (Feb 14 & Feb 21)
Everyone’s favourite, creepy cabaret fringe uncle/urban legend is back – bigger, badder, bulgier than ever. Besides coordinating all of the Noodle Palace shows and running the Late Night Gala, Tomás is also playing a valentine’s day mega show as well as ENDING THE ENTIRE FRINGE FESTIVAL with Tomás Ford Is The End Of The Fringe.
Keith the Anger Management Koala will be playing both the Valentines Day and the End of Fringe shows for Tomás, as well as a raft of other gigs throughout the whole fringe that I’ll put on the “Upcoming” page shortly. In the meantime go out, step beyond your comfort zone, and support some incredible talent by witnessing their abject on-stage madness.

content: AUTHOR’S NOTE: I’ve broken this up into two posts because the original was just waaaay too big. “Part 2: Australia” will be published once my fingers recover. Looking back, the last Mighty Ginge update was August 29th: to say a lot has happened since seeing Chris Hadfield in Canberra is a gross understatement. You probably could have followed some of it via the fairly consistent Instagram, Facebook & Twitter updates, but here’s my vague attempt to sum up the two months of utter chaos that was the European & Australian tour of Becoming Martian. **Germany (August 29th-September 1st) ** Meet “Identity Crisis Bear” Berlin was supposed to be a breather. But coming off the flight from Doha what it really devolved into was a mad dash to try to find three things: 1. WiFi to write & submit a proposal for a payload on a Mars lander 2. A printer to print my train ticket onward to Cologne 3. Food/Sleep In that order of priority. The initial submission deadline for Mars One’s University Competition was August 31st, so I had 24 hours to write an outline for the Helena payload – a scientific payload proposal to generate oxygen from the water in the Martian soil, that also includes a digital art library to Mars. In the process of trying to find wifi to access the payload reference documents I got to wander around Berlin a little, but since I’d visited before in late 2006 I was primarily just trying to find a cafe that I didn’t need a translator to ask for the wifi password… Even with the help of some friendly German cafes, the proposal still wasn’t written by the time I needed to board the train to Cologne. So I ended up writing and submitting a payload proposal for a Mars lander minutes before the deadline using the wifi on the train as it raced through the German countryside at over 230km/hr… Welcome to the future In Cologne I was back in more familiar territory, having stayed there for a few days last November while visiting Europe for the 2013 Living On Mars Convention. Not that I had time to enjoy the familiar sights – I crashed as soon as I checked in, and was up early the next day to visit the European Astronaut Centre! Do you know the way to astronaut street? One of my fellow Mars One candidates Andrea Boyd is EUROCOM – the European Space Agency’s communicator to the International Space Station. So she invited me to see where the European Space Agency’s astronauts train for expeditions to the space station, and where I could muck around in a Soyuz simulator… Not pictured: Hypoxia-induced hallucinations of George Clooney Netherlands (September 2nd – 8th) There was actually a day or two during the week in the Netherlands where I didn’t have to rush anywhere… but it sure as hell wasn’t the day I arrived. There was barely enough time to drop off my bag in Rotterdam before it was back on a train to The Hague – just making it in time for an event on solar weather hosted by the Netherlands Space Society, featuring ESA Astronaut Andre Kuipers and World Space Week ‘s Executive Director Remco Timmermans. Aurora expeditions with Remco Friday brought more space madness, meeting up with ESA’s Communications Director Juan De Dalmau for a tour of the European Space Research and Technology Centre (ESTEC) with fellow International Space University alumni. Me being a “Price Is Right” showgirl for ESA’s next spaceship The ESTEC visit had to be cut short though, because the same night the all important Redhead Days festival kicked off. I’d been in the Netherlands a month too late in 2013, so this year was a great chance to catch up with some old faces and see just how much the festival has grown since I last attended in 2012. Redhead Days Launch To be fair I was pretty burnt out by the time I got there, but something with Redhead Days also seemed to have shifted. The atmosphere of having so many redheads in one place from all across the world is still absolutely amazing, but it wasn’t quite the life altering event my first visit was. I’m certainly not the same person I was when I arrived lost at Breda train station two years ago, so maybe it shouldn’t have come as a surprise that there wasn’t the same impact coming back. The pub crawl continued to be the best event of the weekend’s official program, and this year there was the added bonus of trying to meetup for an interview with a French TV crew during it – they eventually found me (slightly more sober) the next day. But the real highlight was ticking off #22 on the 101 Things To Do Before You Die list by going up in a hot-air balloon the Monday the festival finished. Our balloon was obviously the one with the giant smiley face It was brilliant being back for the Redhead Days festival, but more importantly this visit closed out a lot of unfinished business in the Netherlands from the last 2 years. Maybe one day I’ll go back again for a bit of a laugh, but it very much feels like the festival did what it needed to do – starting my transition from a successful but half-hearted comedian, into a fully fledged space advocate. Ireland (September 9th – 14th) If the Netherlands was about closing out unfinished business, Ireland was very much about starting afresh. I’ve been providing support (viaSkype ) to Niamh Shaw as she developed her Dublin Fringe show, so when I found out the premiere of “To Space” was the night after the Redhead Days festival finished I knew it was the perfect chance to finally visit Ireland! Niamh’s premiere was amazing, and it was great to meet so many fantastic people from Ireland’s burgeoning space industry at the drinks afterwards. When Space Gingers Attack One of the completely unexpected parts of the evening was Niamh drawing names out of a hat to win a piece of original space art from Clare Henderson, and suddenly finding I had to tick off another entry from the 101 Things To Do Before You Die list: #92 Own an Original Work of Art Now safely mounted on my office wall The 48 hours in Dublin was awesome, but with only another 4 days to see as much of Ireland as possible it was into the hire car and off to Cork! Fellow Redhead festival-goer Irene had come over to Ireland too, so we shot down to Cork and met up with Joleen Cronin – organiser of the Irish Redhead Festival. Welcome to the Red-olution We also discovered that Cork is infact a magical and never-ending series of multi-story carparks, after inadvertently driving into 4 of them… Endless, ENDLESS, carparks Depending on how everything pans out with Mars One in the next 6 months, there’s a good chance I’ll be heading back to Cork for the 2015 Irish Redhead Festival to lead their “Ginger Ukulele Orchestra”. Whether I’ll be too busy with training to colonise another planet – or if this planet is ready for hundreds of gingers to start playing ukulele together – remains to be seen… Next stop on the flying Irish tour was the Ring of Kerry, where we witnessed panoramas like this: So… pretty… As well as some blatant racism towards my proud gold-loving cousins: As if we need a special crossing point – we’ve got enough gold to OWN the road Driving on to Dingle Bay, the leprechaun abuse stopped but the overwhelming pretty didn’t: View from the hostel’s balcony The western coast of Ireland – please collect your jaw before you leave Most of the time in Kerry & Dingle Bay was spent just trying not to have an aneurysm over the scenery, and we barely saw 1/100th of what the Wild Atlantic Way had to offer. But there was one really important historical stop we managed to squeeze in. Tom Crean was an Irish explorer that partook in some of the greatest Antarctic expeditions of all time: leading a team on Scott’s 1902 Discovery expedition, surviving Scott’s fatal follow-up Terra Nova expedition in 1910, as well as Shackleton’s ill-fated Endurance expedition. But once Crean had earned his 3rd polar medal & served a further 4 years with the Royal Navy, he retired to Annascaul… where he opened a pub. This is a real place that serves “Crean’s Lager”. We had Coke Four days in Ireland isn’t even remotely enough to even explore Dublin properly, let alone Cork, Kerry & Dingle Bay. But Irene had to head back to the US for work and I was off to Northern Ireland for the CultureTECH Festival. We stayed back in Dublin with Niamh Shaw on our last night in Ireland though, and ended the Ireland leg of the trip with Niamh giving me what is easily the best LEGO set ever: XCOR’s Lynx Mark II CultureTECH in Derry, Northern Ireland (September 15th – 19th) The CultureTECH festival in Derry was always going to be the trip’s pressure pot – 3 days as one of the featured speakers for a technology festival with hundreds of events & activities. I wound up staying for 5 days: speaking about Mars One at half a dozen schools that ranged from high-end boarding schools, to running technology workshops, playing Bowie’s “Space Oddity” on ukulele during interviews with BBC radio, performing “Becoming Martian” as a charity event for Children In Crossfire, and talking about having the courage to fail over and over and over again at the Create2014 student-run event. Create2014 – Inspirin’ da yoof with failure It was 5 days of abject chaos… but without a doubt one of the best parts of the entire trip. Because while I was running around like a headless chook trying to keep track of when and where I was, every step of the way there were incredible people to steer me in the right direction. The team from CultureTECH were simply amazing: lining up as many school visits as I could squeeze in, organising interviews with the BBC, and having taxis ready to get me wherever I needed to be. Not only that, they put me up in 5-star accommodation the whole time I was there so I could tick off a third entry from the 101 Things list: #30 “Stay in the Best Suite in a Five Star Hotel”. It wasn’t just the CultureTECH organisers who were awesome either. My old Irish friend Barry had moved back to Derry a few months before, so it was fantastic to finally catch up with him – I’d barely seen Barry since late 2010, when we were sharing a mouldy flat in London and I moved out because my taste in girlfriends had suddenly improved. Without going into specifics Barry has had a particularly rough year, so I think it was good for both of us to catch up and remember that even with the dips he’s had over the last 12 months, life is still way better than it was 4 years ago. Circa December 2010, aka “Evidence Exhibit A” But while we were reminiscing, Barry & I were also causing chaos at the festival and making mountains of friends doing it. CultureTECH had brought in so many inspiring folks from all across the world it was hard to keep track of them all: Heather from Uproar Comics, Alastair from Startacus, the dozen scholarship winners from Honeycomb, and the hysterical team from Ministry of Science … whose children’s shows undoubtedly contain less innuendo than I like to pretend they do. Emma wants to end on a big bang, but Mike isn’t sure they should, in front of all the kids… CulutreTECH was genuinely out of control, and I loved every moment of it – from ridiculous dinner parties that ended with us getting kicked out of the dodgiest pub in Derry, right through to performing “Becoming Martian” while sounding like a koala with emphysema because my voice had gone that morning. It was ridiculous, fun-filled chaos all the way through, and I genuinely hope I get a chance to go back again and do it all again. London, Benenden & Brighton (Sept 20-26) Leaving Northern Ireland was a stark wake up call to the realities of life though… And let us never speak of this again After the nightmare that was my flight out of Belfast to Bristol though, I managed to knock over a bunch of little jobs that I’d been carrying with me since National Science Week. Restitching my bag, sewing patches on my ukulele case, copying all my random scraps of paper covered in ideas into something more permanent… general travel admin. Once you’ve been living out of a bag for a few weeks there’s often a moment where you realise things are going to start falling apart on you if you don’t take a little time to fix them – landing in Bristol was that moment, so on the bus to Bath I sorted everything. Things would start falling apart again before I got back to Perth, but that’s another story. The return to Gloucestershire was very short though. I managed to catch up with Vicky & Olly – two great friends from my days working for Damien Hirst – for a few hours in Bath. But the next morning the infamous Martin picked me up for breakfast in my old town of Stroud, I managed to catch up with Mark Chatterley from InEarEntertainment for a few hours, then it was on the move again down to London that afternoon… For tourists, this is a delightful photo op. For anyone who’s spent 6 hours waiting for a 5am train, this sign causes a rash London was another rushed, overnight visit – caught up briefly with John & Jo to see what wonderful things they’d been doing post Edinburgh Fringe, but the very next morning it was off to speak to the students at the exclusive Benenden boarding school in country Kent. The kids and staff were brilliant, really enthusiastic about World Space Week, and I even managed to find a fellow ukulele-er among the staff! The compulsion to play “Duelling Banjos” was significant But Benenden was really just a fun detour for where I really wanted to be, was here… Into the Temple of (burrito) Sacrifice … with it’s amazing interior decorations… Mexican eating establishment protected by The Space Jesus Last stop of the Europe leg was back to that other old stomping ground of mine: Brighton, with the best burritos on the planet at La Choza. The world’s best housemate, Megan – whose garage I was living in when I decided to sign up for Mars One at the end of September 2012 – put me up for a few nights while I prepared for the return to Australia, partaking in all the awesome food and coffee Brighton has to offer at the same time. And in amongst it all I even managed to get up to London again to catch up with Lizzy from Ginger Parrot at an open mic cabaret night in an underground toilet. With all of that going on, you’d think it would be time to go home and have a bit of a nap. And if you call all of Australia home, then yeah I did go home – “home” to run a space conference in Adelaide, present at a different space conference, speak & perform at a Newcastle writer’s festival, dress up like an aluminium-foil covered robot with plastic cups for boobs, bolt up to Brisbane to speak at schools & universities, as well as meeting dozens more amazing people along the way. But I guess that will all have to wait until the epic conclusion of Josh’s Europe/Oz Odyssey… This Odyssey involves considerably less scurvy… - Paul Ahhh EasyJet.
