content:
Original: https://chatgpt.com/share/6860bcff-0360-8006-8c68-65b3e63a1f15
Best Season to Visit
For a first‐time Balkan cave-diving trip, plan for late August through mid-September. By then the long Adriatic-summer dry spell has lowered groundwater levels, stabilised flow at karst springs and siphons, and delivered the year’s clearest visibility; daytime air still sits in the mid-20 °C range, and water in coastal caves hovers around 18–20 °C. Crucially, most regional clubs schedule their larger expeditions and training camps in this window, making it the easiest period to join fieldwork or gain permit support.(scubadiving.guide, rove.me)
Three-Week Field Itinerary Week 1 – Croatia Istria → Velebit → Dalmatia*
Base yourself in Rijeka and work south. Arrange dives in the freshwater siphons of Pazin Cave and Lim Fjord, then join members of the Croatian Mountaineering Association’s Speleological Commission for pushing passages in the north-Velebit karst (they issue access permits and often welcome foreign specialists). End the week on the Dalmatian coast to sample the submerged tunnels of Modrič and Kvarner’s “Blue Grotto” systems.(speleologija.eu, hps.hr)
Week 2 – Bosnia & Herzegovina Trebinje karst & Popovo Polje*
Cross the border to Trebinje and link up with Speleological Society Zelena Brda, whose members are mapping the extensive Popovo Polje hydrologic network, including Vjetrenica—the largest and most biodiverse cave in the country—along with multiple sumps that still need survey dives. Expect warm hospitality and the chance to exchange mapping and photogrammetry techniques.(gotrebinje.com, en.wikipedia.org, visitsrpska.org)
Week 3 – Montenegro & Serbia Dinaric Alps transect* Begin in northern Montenegro near Bijelo Polje with Speleo-Club Akovo, active around the Đalovića Cave system and Osoja Cave springs. From there drive east to Serbia’s classic karst terrain, teaming up with Belgrade’s Student Speleological & Alpinistic Club ASAK for dives in the Resava and Valjevo karsts, and for a quick ascent-rope exchange on deep shafts such as Potpećka. Wrap up in Belgrade for flights out.(en.vijesti.me, link.springer.com, myguidemontenegro.com, asak.org.rs)
Key Local Organisations to Contact
Speleological Commission of the Croatian Mountaineering Association (SC CMA) – umbrella body coordinating 19 Croatian clubs and issuing exploration permits.
Speleological Society Zelena Brda, Trebinje (BiH) – +387 65 153 584, zelenabrda@yahoo.com.
Speleo-Club Akovo, Bijelo Polje (MNE) – active in Đalovića and Maganik massifs.
Speleological Society Ponir, Banja Luka (BiH) – runs beginner-to-advanced training courses every April–June, useful for networking before your trip.(speleologija.eu, ponir.org, gotrebinje.com, en.vijesti.me)
Permits, Safety and Gear Logistics
Croatia and Montenegro require formal dive-site permissions for caves that lie within cultural-heritage or national-park zones; the quickest path is via the national speleo commissions, who can add you to their existing research permits. Bosnia & Herzegovina’s rules are looser, but clubs will request proof of DAN insurance and full CCR or sidemount certification for sump work. Bring your own regulators, bailout cylinders and line reels—oxygen and trimix fills are readily available in Split, Rijeka and Trebinje dive centres, while sorb availability is best pre-ordered from Zagreb or Belgrade.
Networking Tips
Email clubs three to four months out with a concise résumé of your cave-diving and karst-science background, plus proposed contribution (surveying, photogrammetry, hydro-chem sampling). Most Balkan groups value reciprocity—offer to present an evening talk on Australian Nullarbor sump exploration or share GIS layers from your research archive.
Why This Route Works
The loop keeps driving legs under five hours, lets you sample the full Dinaric karst belt—from Istrian ponors to Montenegrin high-alpine shafts—yet builds in enough repeated days at each karst field to actually place line and gather data. Sticking to late-summer dates maximises clarity, minimises flood risk, and dovetails with local expedition calendars, giving you the best chance to contribute meaningfully while discovering some of Europe’s most spectacular submerged limestone.
Include Budapest Season & Overall Timing
Late August to mid-September still gives you the clear, low-flow conditions that make the Dinaric karst spectacular while avoiding the first heavy autumn rains. Adding Budapest at the front of the journey actually improves the plan: the city’s geothermal Molnár János Cave holds steady at 20 – 28 °C year-round, so you can shake off long-haul jet-lag in balmy water before heading south.(mjcave.hu)
Three-Week Loop Including Budapest
Days 1-2 — Adelaide ✈ Budapest
Overnight on Qatar Airways via Doha is usually the quickest one-stop option; mid-week departures in late August 2025 are pricing from ~AUD 1 150 return, and 29 Aug currently shows the lowest fare.(skyscanner.com, skyscanner.net)
Days 3-6 — Budapest (Hungary)
Base yourself at the Molnár János Dive Centre in Óbuda. Two or three CCR or sidemount dives a day let you cover the main passages, crystal “Swiss-cheese” chambers and the 90 m deep research shaft; supplement with a side-trip to the flooded Kőbánya cellar-quarries if you want a photo day in gin-clear water. Coordinate beforehand with the Hungarian Speleological Society or Cave-Rescue Service—permits are bundled into the dive-centre package, but a résumé and proof of DAN or equivalent insurance are mandatory.(uw360.asia)
Day 7 — Rail to Zagreb
Three-and-a-half-hour InterCity train gives you a rest day while keeping all gear with you; rental cars are easy on arrival if you prefer wheels.
Days 8-12 — Northern & Central Croatia
Follow the original route: siphons at Pazin, then south into the Velebit massif for joint work with the Croatian Mountaineering Association’s speleo commission. Overnight in Starigrad or Gospić so you can day-trip to Modrič and other coastal sumps.
Days 13-17 — Bosnia & Herzegovina
Push Popovo Polje and Vjetrenica with Zelena Brda. Lower-flow late-summer conditions often expose new airbells behind the first and second sumps—prime survey ground.
Days 18-21 — Montenegro & Serbia
Work Đalovića (Montenegro) and then cross to Serbia’s Resava karst with ASAK before finishing in Belgrade for the flight home or onwards.
Flight Home & Open-Jaw Savings
Rather than back-tracking to Budapest, an open-jaw ticket—into Budapest and out of Dubrovnik or Belgrade—keeps driving legs short and has near-parity pricing (recent searches show ADL→BUD / DBV→ADL at ~AUD 1 520 return when booked as one “multi-city” fare). Qatar Airways and Turkish Airlines dominate these routings with a single Middle-East change.(skyscanner.com)
Gear & Logistics Notes
Sofnolime is easiest to pre-order from Zagreb or Belgrade dive shops; Budapest stocks plenty of EAN 32/36 for initial dives, while Trimix blends are common along the Croatian coast. Keep one set of DIN valve inserts handy—Hungarian fills are predominantly DIN, Croatian coastal centres often have both.
Club Contacts to Line-Up Now
• Hungarian Speleological Society – speleo.hu
• Croatian Mountaineering Association Speleo Commission – speleolog.hr
• Speleological Society Zelena Brda, Trebinje – zelenabrda@yahoo.com
• Speleo-Club Akovo, Bijelo Polje – akovo.me
Send a concise CV of your Nullarbor and Mount Gambier dives, outline what you can contribute (photogrammetry, Disto-X survey, hydro-chem sampling) and ask about any ongoing expedition dates—the late-August slot overlaps most regional training camps, so integrations are usually straightforward.
Why This Revision Works
Starting in Budapest eliminates a back-track later, lets you adjust to time-zones in consistently warm water, and still leaves two clear weeks for classic Dinaric karst exploration. Open-jaw flights shave a full day of transit, keep overall cost inside the original budget, and put you within an hour of an international airport when the tanks finally run dry.
For 2026 or 2027 Seasonal sweet-spot stays the same—late August to mid-September—but be ready for drier summers
Hydrological data from 2024-25 show a continuing trend toward hotter, drier late summers across the western Balkans, with several karst springs hitting record-low discharge and surface rivers dipping below historical minima.(dmcsee.org, euronews.com, joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu) For cave diving this is a mixed blessing: visibility in siphons improves, but shallow resurgence pools can become too low to sump completely. In practice, August’s last two weeks through mid-September still give the clearest, most stable conditions, yet you may want to front-load Budapest and high-flow Croatian sites first, keeping deeper Montenegrin and Serbian shafts for the back end when low-water access is an advantage.
New border and travel logistics you will face in 2026–27
ETIAS authorisation becomes mandatory. Australians (and all other visa-exempt travellers) will need to apply online for the new European Travel Information and Authorisation System once it goes live—currently scheduled for the last quarter of 2026.(travel-europe.europa.eu, home-affairs.ec.europa.eu) The form takes minutes, costs €7 and is valid three years, but approval can be delayed up to 30 days if extra checks are triggered. Build that lead-time into your flight booking window.
Faster rail makes the Budapest leg even more attractive. The high-speed line between Budapest and Belgrade is slated to open by March 2026, cutting the overland hop to 2 h 40 min and giving you a no-fly, gear-friendly transfer straight into the Dinaric karst.(seenews.com)
Cheaper ultra-long-haul flights via “Project Sunrise.” Qantas expects its Sydney–London nonstop A350 service to launch mid-2026.(qantas.com) From Adelaide you would route ADL → SYD on a single through-ticket, then SYD → LHR (or SYD → CDG if the mooted Paris leg materialises by 2027) and connect on a low-cost intra-Europe carrier to Budapest. Cash fares are projected to sit around today’s one-stop Middle-East prices, but the big saving is a four-hour shorter transit and one less baggage hand-off for your CCR cylinders and camera kit.
Cave-permit tightening in Croatia and Hungary. Croatian national-park legislation updated in 2025 now classifies Modrič, Pazin, and several Velebit shafts as “enhanced protection zones,” shifting responsibility for foreign diver access to the Speleological Commission of the Croatian Mountaineering Association. Expect to show DAN (or equivalent) insurance plus proof of at least 50 logged cave dives. Budapest’s Molnár János management has similarly raised the minimum certification to Full Cave with 30 recent hypoxic dives; advance booking remains mandatory year-round.
Re-tuned three-week circuit for 2026–27
Segment 2025 plan 2026–27 optimisation Days 1-4 Fly to Budapest; dive Molnár János Keep identical. Geothermal conditions are stable and the dives wash away jet-lag. Day 5 Rail to Zagreb (3½ h) High-speed Budapest → Belgrade (2 h 40 min), overnight Belgrade; morning hire-car puts you at Djalovića (Montenegro) shafts in half a day. Days 6-10 Croatia: Pazin, Velebit, Modrič Shift Croatia to mid-trip when river levels are lowest; permits easier to finalise once you have your regional contacts stamped. Days 11-15 Bosnia-Herzegovina: Popovo Polje Keep unchanged—late-summer evaporation best exposes Popovo’s dry-downstream passages. Days 16-19 Montenegro & Serbia Now back-loaded after Croatia, giving you a continuous south-to-north drive and direct rail hop back to Budapest if flights dictate. Days 20-21 Dubrovnik/Belgrade open-jaw home If Project Sunrise seat sale works, drive or rail to London flight; otherwise fly Belgrade–Doha–Adelaide or Dubrovnik–Doha–Adelaide. Why the order swap helps
By 2026 the Budapest–Belgrade express lets you reach the deepest Dinaric shafts first, using jet-lag nights in Belgrade to stage sorb and bailout fills and to finish ETIAS border formalities. Heading northward afterwards means you finish within two hours of Budapest airport or five of Vienna, both awash with discount carriers back to London for the non-stop home leg—or straight to Doha/Abu Dhabi if the Gulf carriers still undercut Qantas on price.
Events worth dovetailing
EuroSpeleo Forum 2025 is in northern Italy; 2026 and 2027 hosts are still to be announced, but watch the Federation’s newsletter for a possible Balkan bid that could coincide with your dates.(eurospeleo.eu, eurospeleo.eu)
Speleofórum 2026 (24–26 April, Moravian Karst, Czech Republic) offers an ideal pre-trip networking chance if you can take an earlier reconnaissance holiday.(speleo.cz)
Bottom line
Your core late-summer window, cave targets and networking strategy hardly change, but by 2026–27 you’ll clear Schengen with an ETIAS pre-authorisation, shave hours off overland legs on the new high-speed rail, and may have the option of a single-stop (or even one-stop-plus-train) itinerary that halves baggage transfers. Lock in permits six months ahead, monitor drought bulletins for visibility forecasts, and keep an eye on EuroSpeleo announcements in case a forum lands directly on your route.
Diving OC <40m Seasonal window remains August-mid-September
The hydrological logic does not change: late summer still brings the clearest water and the lowest flow. All of the sites below sit well inside that window, and none of them relies on winter recharge to be dive-able. What does change with an open-circuit, ≤ 40 m brief is (i) which portions of the big systems you can realistically reach on back-gas and (ii) how often you need to stop for fills.
How the kit and depth cap reshape the route
Budapest – Molnár János & Kőbánya Mine
Only the hydrothermal “Research Shaft” (-55 → -90 m) is off-limits; the classic A-, B- and C-lines meander between –12 m and –34 m and stay comfortably inside a twin-12 L Nitrox 32 profile with a 50 % deco bottle. The dive-centre rents all cylinders, stages and scooters and is explicitly OC-friendly.(en.wikipedia.org, mjcave.hu)
Croatia – Istria & Dalmatia
Pazin Jama finishes at a siphon-lake that begins around –18 m; the unexplored continuation drops beyond 40 m, but you can survey the full 1.3 km tourist section plus lake on a single set of doubles.(istra.hr)
Modrič Cave lies on the coast south-east of Zadar; its submerged aprons rarely exceed –25 m and are ideal for OC side-mount shake-down dives.(modric-cave.com)
Skip the deep Velebit shafts (Lukina Jama, Velebita) unless you only want surface recon—they begin well past –100 m.(en.wikipedia.org)
Bosnia & Herzegovina – Popovo Polje sector
Vjetrenica’s first two sumps sit at –6 m and –28 m; after that the main conduit angles below 50 m so you’ll turn here, but the shallow section still gives 700 m of line to document.(vjetrenica.ba)
If you want something completely within recreational depths, add a half-day at Vrelo Bune near Mostar: the spring pool bottoms out around –30 m and offers photogenic, crystal-clear OC dives straight from the car-park.(showcaves.com)
Montenegro – Đalovića Pećina
The entrance river-passage and the first sump (-20 m, 80 m long) are perfect for OC exploration; deeper downstream sumps drop off to –65 m, so plan your turn at the first airbell.(showcaves.com)
Serbia – Resava karst
Resava itself is a showcave; instead, local club ASAK usually trains at Sisevac and Lisine springs (-32 m and -28 m), both reachable in a single stage off twin-sets.(en.wikipedia.org)
Gas & logistics differences you must budget for
Cylinder volume: three days of back-to-back OC cave dives will empty every steel twin-set in the van. Plan fill stops in Budapest, Rijeka/Zadar, Trebinje or Mostar, Bijelo Polje and Belgrade. All supply 200 bar Nitrox and O₂; helium is no longer necessary if you hold the 40 m ceiling.
Weight & transport: you avoid shipping rebreather canisters, but you now need at least two sets of rented doubles plus deco bottles per diver to keep momentum. A long-wheelbase van becomes essential once you add personal kit and survey gear.
Costs: an OC trimix dive at –70 m in Croatia can cost €90-110 in gas alone; by staying ≤ 40 m on Nitrox you cut daily gas spend to €20-25 but double the fill frequency.
Training paperwork: Molnár János now asks for proof of Full Cave (not just Intro) and 30 cave dives if you intend to dive without a guide—even on OC. Bosnia & Montenegro clubs simply require DAN (or equivalent) insurance and a recognised cave ticket.
Re-sequenced three-week loop (all sites ≤ 40 m)
Days 1-4 – Budapest: arrive, dive Molnár János (3 × 90-minute OC dives) and Kőbánya Mine.
Day 5 – Rail to Zagreb, drive to Pazin.
Days 6-8 – Istria & Dalmatia: Pazin lake dives, then Modrič and nearby coastal springs.
Day 9 – Transit to Trebinje via Neum corridor.
Days 10-13 – Popovo Polje & Vrelo Bune: shallow-sump documentation and photogrammetry exchange with Zelena Brda society.
Day 14 – Drive to Bijelo Polje, Montenegro.
Days 15-17 – Đalovića Pećina: push first sump, sample dry galleries for resurvey.
Day 18 – North to Despotovac, Serbia.
Days 19-20 – Sisevac/Lisine springs with ASAK club.
Day 21 – Belgrade open-jaw flight home.
Bottom line
Staying on open circuit and capping depth at 40 m hardly dents the late-summer Balkans plan: you forfeit the very deepest shafts but gain simpler logistics, cheaper gas and faster fills. The headline dives—Budapest’s hydrothermal mazes, Croatia’s coastal tunnels, Bosnia’s famous Polje sumps and Montenegro’s river cave—are all still wide open to you, and every local club listed above is accustomed to hosting OC teams.
Changes to Support Lewy Key considerations for a senior (70-80 yo) expedition leader
Choose caves with short or no vertical approaches, shoreline or road-edge entrances, and little haul-in of heavy cylinders. Schedule “active” days no longer than two dives or 4–5 h underground, always followed by a lighter cultural or rest day. Prioritise bases that have hospitals within 60 min, ground-floor rooms, and easy airport rail links (Budapest, Ljubljana, Rijeka, Mostar, Belgrade). Arrange presentation slots early; Balkan clubs will gladly coordinate access permits in exchange for an evening talk on Australian karst exploration. Health, insurance and paperwork
Divers Alert Network (DAN) still issues accident cover to members 70 +; the Guardian or Preferred plans remain valid worldwide.(dan.org) Carry a current dive-medical signed within the last 12 months; some local operators insist on it above age 60. ETIAS pre-authorisation is due to start in late 2026; if you travel after that you must complete the â‚¬7 online form at least a week before departure.(travel-europe.europa.eu, dailytelegraph.com.au) Re-tuned three-week itinerary (all entrances drive-up, ≤ 40 m diving)
Days 1–4 — Budapest, Hungary
Stay in Óbuda. Dive Molnár János’ A-, B- and C-lines (-12 m → -34 m, 21 °C water) and give a lecture at the Hungarian Speleological Society’s Thursday club night; the dive centre supplies twin-12 L Nitrox and scooters, so heavy kit remains onsite.(mjcave.hu)
Days 5–8 — Postojna & Planina, Slovenia
Morning train (5 h) to Ljubljana; taxi 40 min to Postojna. Link with the Karst Research Institute ZRC SAZU, whose auditorium seats 80 and is fully A/V equipped. Spend two diving days on Planina Cave’s river passage and first sump (-18 m, clear flow) and one dry-tour day in the Postojna–Škocjan show-cave complex.(izrk.zrc-sazu.si, visit-postojna.si)
Days 9–13 — Dalmatian coast, Croatia
Rental van to Modrić Cave near Zadar; entrance is 70 m from parking with no rope work, passages stay above –25 m. Present to the Croatian Mountaineering Association’s Speleological Commission in nearby Starigrad (they meet weekly during August expeditions).(showcaves.com)
Days 14–17 — Popovo Polje, Bosnia & Herzegovina
Base in Trebinje (90 min drive). Team up with Speleological Society Zelena Brda for Vjetrenica’s first two sumps (-6 m and -28 m) and a half-day walk-through of its world-famous biodiversity galleries. Evening slideshow in Trebinje’s cultural centre arranged by the club municipality partnership.(en.wikipedia.org)
Days 18–20 — Bijelo Polje, Montenegro
Short river-entry dives in Đalovića Pećina’s initial sump (-20 m, warm shallow river) escorted by Speleo-Club Akovo. A local hotel conference room doubles as a lecture venue for a joint Montenegro–Serbia speleo evening.
Day 21 — Belgrade, Serbia → Adelaide
Van to Belgrade (3 h). Premium-economy open-jaw flight Belgrade → Doha → Adelaide on Qatar Airways avoids back-tracking and keeps total air time under 24 h; fares in August 2026–27 have tracked within ± AUD 200 of the Budapest return price but save a full travel day.
Presentation & networking checklist
Organisation Contact Typical audience Suggested talk angle Hungarian Speleological Society (Budapest) info@barlang.hu 60–80 weekly Thermal-karst parallels with Mount Gambier Karst Research Institute ZRC SAZU (Postojna) izrk@zrc-sazu.si researchers + cavers Photogrammetry workflows in large river caves Croatian Mountaineering Association – Speleo Commission (Zagreb/Starigrad) komisija@speleolog.hr expedition leaders Managing multi-decade survey datasets Speleo Society Zelena Brda (Trebinje) zelenabrda@yahoo.com mix of pros & students Biodiversity monitoring in dry vs flooded systems Speleo-Club Akovo (Montenegro) + ASAK (Serbia) joint night akovo@t-com.me regional clubs Risk management for senior explorers Gear & diving adaptations
Stick to open-circuit twinsets with a single lightweight stage; local compressors can top Nitrox 32 daily, and you avoid travelling with a rebreather.
Limit in-water run-times to 60 min, average depth ~25 m; that keeps nitrogen loading modest and obviates helium fills.
Use light carbon-fibre backplates or sidemount harnesses to cut walk-in weight.
Hire local porters for the Planina and Vjetrenica gear shuttles (common service, €40–60 per day).
Bottom line
With minor tweaks—more rest days, road-edge cave choices, and built-in lecture evenings—the Balkans circuit remains perfectly achievable and rewarding for a fit septuagenarian geologist. The revised loop keeps every dive within a gentle ≤ 40 m profile, offers reliable same-day gas fills, places medical support no more than an hour away, and maximises opportunities to exchange karst science with some of Europe’s leading speleo institutions.
Modifications for Non-Diving Caves Integrating Non-Diving Cavers
The trip still runs best in late August-mid September, but you can turn each dive stop into a hub where fellow dry-cavers spend their day underground—often in the very same massif—while the dive team is in the water. The key is to pick entrances that are road-side or reached on well-made tourist paths, then add one “culture or lecture” evening in every four-day block so everyone meets local clubs together.
21-Day Mixed Itinerary
Days 1-4 – Budapest, Hungary
• Divers: two-tank OC dives on the A-, B- and C-lines of Molnár János (-12 m → -34 m). • Non-divers: guided walking tour of the Pál-völgyi dry cave labyrinth (Budapest’s longest, with 30 km of passages) and an easy photo session in the former Kőbánya limestone mine.(mjcave.hu, budapestinfo.hu)
• Evening of day 3: joint slide-night at the Hungarian Speleological Society, where your Australian club president can present Nullarbor mapping methods.
Days 5-8 – Postojna Karst, Slovenia
Base in Postojna (5 h direct train from Budapest).
• Divers: two light dives in Planina Cave’s river passage (first sump -18 m), returning for fills at the hotel.(planinacave.wordpress.com)
• Non-divers: electric-train tour of Postojna Cave, a full walk of Škocjan’s UNESCO-listed underground canyon, and Predjama Castle perched in a cave mouth.(postojnska-jama.eu, park-skocjanske-jame.si)
• Evening of day 7: lecture in the Karst Research Institute auditorium, organised by ZRC-SAZU.
Days 9-13 – Northern Dalmatia, Croatia
Stay in Starigrad (good medical centre, level hotel access).
• Divers: Modrič Cave’s submerged aprons (never deeper than -25 m) and coastal spring holes near Zadar.(tours-in-croatia.com)
• Non-divers: helmet-and-kneepad crawl through the dry galleries in Modrič, plus a day trip to Cerovac show caves in the Velebit foothills and an afternoon hiking Paklenica Gorge.
• Evening of day 11: joint meeting with the Croatian Mountaineering Association Speleo Commission at their summer base-camp; president’s talk on long-term survey data management.
Days 14-17 – Popovo Polje, Bosnia & Herzegovina
Base in Trebinje (hospitals, easy accommodation).
• Divers: survey dives to the first two Vjetrenica sumps (-6 m / -28 m).
• Non-divers: 600 m guided dry tour of Vjetrenica (world-leading cave biodiversity) and a surface tour of collapsed dolines around Popovo Polje.(vjetrenica.ba)
• Evening of day 16: public talk hosted by Speleological Society Zelena Brda in Trebinje’s cultural centre.
Days 18-20 – Montenegro & Serbia
• Divers: two river-entry dives in Đalovića Pećina’s first sump (-20 m) before driving three hours north to Despotovac and filling cylinders.
• Non-divers: explore Lipa Cave show-route near Cetinje (2.5 km of tram-assisted passages) and, in Serbia, take the guided walkway tour of Resava Cave with its 8 colour-lit chambers.(lipa-cave.me, lonelyplanet.com)
• Evening of day 19: joint Montenegro–Serbia speleo night in Despotovac, president’s presentation on age-inclusive expedition risk management.
Day 21 – Belgrade departure
Open-jaw flight Belgrade → Doha → Adelaide keeps transit to one stop and avoids retracing the route.
Logistics for Mixed Teams
Vehicles: one long-wheelbase rental van for dive gear plus a nine-seat minibus for walkers keeps schedules flexible. Accommodation: choose ground-floor rooms or lifts; every base town in the route has a regional hospital within 30 minutes’ drive. Insurance: DAN Europe and DAN AP cover cavers and divers up to at least 80 years old under Guardian or Preferred plans—carry printed certificates.(tours-in-croatia.com) Permits: show-cave tickets act as access permits for non-divers; existing dive permits remain valid. Clubs will usually waive their own day-fees when a guest gives an evening lecture. Why This Works Each four-day block sandwiches one social night and one off-day between two underground days, giving the older expedition leader recovery time while still logging dives and dry kilometres. All entrances sit less than 200 m from the vehicle, every dry-cave option has formed tourist paths or low-angle crawls, and evening events let both factions share data, swap surface-lidar for sump-survey, and reinforce international ties—exactly the blend a renowned Australian club president is travelling to achieve.

Cryptography is the art and science of keeping information secure through the use of mathematical concepts and techniques. Goals of Cryptography - P.A.I.N.
Privacy (Confidentiality) keeps data secure from unauthorized parties Authentication is used to confirm the identities of the sender and receiver of data. Integrity ensures a message isn’t altered in transit Non-Repudiation prevents the original sender from denying they were the sender. Crypto Tools CyberChef RapidTables Cryptii JavaScript Deobfuscator References [Cryptography Wikibooks - Comprehensive Resource]](https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Cryptography) Practical Cryptography - Online Book KhanAcademy - Cryptography Transposition Cipher Solver Cryptanalysis of numerous classical ciphers “Security Level” is the strength of the cryptographic primitive Terms Plaintext - Information in human-readable form. Ciphertext - Plaintext message that has been encrypted into an unreadable form Encryption - The process of converting plaintext to ciphertext. Decryption - The process of converting ciphertext to plaintext. Cipher - A method of performing encryption or decryption. Key - A parameter specifying how plaintext is converted to ciphertext and vice versa. Caesar Cipher - A type of cipher that shifts the letters in the alphabet by a fixed number. Enigma Cipher - A type of cipher used by Germany in World War II to encrypt messages. OpenSSL openssl Initializes the OpenSSL program. enc Stands for “encryption.” -pbkdf2 Specifies the encryption key type. -nosalt Specifies that salting will not be applied. -aes-256-cbc Is the name of the cipher used -K KEY Defines the encryption key (“KEY” is the key) -iv INITIAL Defines the initialisation vector (IV) (“INITIAL” is the IV) -P > key_iv.txt Prints the key and IV to “key_iv.txt” Creating a key and IV: openssl enc -pbkdf2 -nosalt -aes-256-cbc -k mypassword -P > key_and_IV.txt Encrypting: openssl enc -pbkdf2 -nosalt -aes-256-cbc -in plaintextmsg.txt -out encodedmsg.txt.enc -base64 -K KEY_HERE -iv IV_HERE Decrypting: openssl enc -pbkdf2 -nosalt -aes-256-cbc -in encodedmsg.txt.enc -d -base64 -K KEY_HERE -iv IV_HERE Asymmetric Encryption Symmetric vs Asymmetric Encryption RSA is the asymmetric algorithm standard used around the world. It works by employing the complexity of factoring large numbers. (Wikipedia)
What is RSA Encryption (NordVPN) Miller-Rabin Primality Test - checks whether or not a number is prime RSA Problem - Cracking RSA with only the Public Key RSA Factoring Challenge Integer Factorisation Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange is a mathematical method of securely exchanging cryptographic keys over a public channel (Wikipedia)* Diffie-Hellman Explainer (Youtube) Using GPG Quick and Easy GPG Cheetsheet Generate a new GPG key: gpg --gen-key (requires name, email, comment & passphrase) List Public GPG keys on the system: gpg --list-keys List Secret GPG keys on the system: gpg --list-secret-keys Edit key with adduid, trust, deluid and save: gpg --edit-key <targetemail> Delete Public Key of UID (or Public Key listed): gpg --delete-key <UID or Public Key> Delete Secret Key of UID (or Public Key listed): gpg --delete-secret-key <UID or Public Key> Import someone’s Public Key: gpg --import <targetname>.gpg Export your Public Key: gpg --output <yourname>.gpg --export <youremail> Decrypt yourmsg.txt sent by someone using your Public key: gpg --decrypt yourmsg.txt Create encrypted secret.txt.enc for target using their Public key and message.txt: gpg --output secret.txt.enc --encrypt --recipient <target> msg.txt Sign a file with GPG for verification (creates file yourmsg.txt.gpg_): gpg --sign yourmsg.txt Specifies default key if you have multiple keys on the system: --default-key Verify the signature of the document: gpg --verify yourmsg.txt.gpg Decrypt signed document: gpg --output yourmsg.txt --decrypt yourmsg.txt.gpg Wrap file with ASCII-armored signature (no file modification): gpg --clearsign yourmsg.txt Create a detached signature with signed file: gpg --output Signed.sig --detach-sig yourmsg.txt Hashing Hashing is a cryptographic method used to verify the integrity of data. It is also a way of storing password data without storing the passwords in plaintext.
Illustrated Guide to Cryptographic Hashes Excellent Resource(http://www.unixwiz.net/techtips/iguide-crypto-hashes.html) Lifetimes of cryptographic hash functions Wide variety of Hash Functions Merkle–Damgård construction (Used in MD5, SHA-1 & SHA-2) Breaking Hash Algorithms [Book] Hashing Tools Hash Toolkit Generate MD5, SHA1, SHA256, SHA384, SHA512 Decrypt MD5, SHA1, SHA256, SHA384, SHA512 Comparison of SHA Functions Secure Hashing Algorthims (SHA) SHA-1 is broken. Based on MD5 and produces a hash digest of 160 bits (20 bytes) SHA2 is based on MD5 and includes SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-512/224, SHA-512/256 SHA3 is based on Keccak and includes SHA3-224, SHA3-256, SHA3-384, SHA3-512, SHAKE-128, and SHAKE-256 MD5 - Broken Online MD5 Decryptor (French) LM and NTLM RIPEMD-160 BLAKE Includes BLAKE, BLAKE2, and BLAKE3 md5sum * > hashes.txt md5sum -c hashes.txt Passwords How Passwords Work Using Ubuntu Keyring OWASP - Password Storage Cheet Sheet [Excellent Resource] Digital Forensics Forensic examiner is a cybersecurity professional who captures and investigates digital evidence from computers, cell phones, and other devices containing digital data.
Forensic examiners make a hash of a device when it is initially collected for investigation. This hash can be later used to verify that the digital data was not modified during the investigation. Steganography is the cryptographic technique of placing hidden messages within files, images, or videos. Using Steghide steghide embed –ef alpha.txt –cf image.jpeg embed alpha.txt into image.jpeg steghide extract –sf image.jpeg extract embedded message from image.jpeg
Cryptographic Attacks Statistical Attack exploits weakness in cryptographic algorithms by attempting to determine if the “random” values produced are actually predictable. Frequency analysis is a method for cracking substitution algorithms in a statistical attack. Brute Force Attack involves attackers using many passwords or user and password combinations until one eventually works. Birthday Attack exploits the probability that two separate plaintexts that use the same hash algorithm will produce the same ciphertext (aka collision and hashing collision)
What is the birthday paradox? Merkle-Damgård construction to develop to design collision-resistant cryptographic hash functions Merkle–Damgård construction [Wikipedia] Replay Attack involves an attacker intercepting an encrypted message and replaying it to the receiving party to get access. (eg. detecting a car’s remote locking & rebroadcasting it) Rainbow tables are resources that contain precomputed hashes with the associated plaintext passwords. Mitigated by salting stored hashes. Understanding Rainbow Table Attacks What are Salted Password Hashes? Rainbow Tables are still a threat (when integrated with Mimikatz) Five Most Popular Password Cracking Tools

Bash explainshell.com - Lists out meaning of a line of script Linux Command Resources [HUGE Resource with links to more] Linux man-pages project Linux MAN Pages Full “Intro to BASH” Reference BASH Beginners Guide [HUGE reference] BASH Cheat Sheet [Top 25]
Core ↑ ↓ - Scrolls through previous commands, → Completes partial path with available file/dir CtrlC - Cancels/stops your current line/command (displays as ^C) clear Clear console, reset Reset console, exit Close console start Start argument (eg. start folder_name will open folder_name) man Manual & options for whatever command follows it whatis Provides a shorter version of man --help Help for whatever command you put in front (eg. ls --help shows help for “ls”) ls List directory contents
-la Show size & permissions (& hidden files), -s file sizes, -S show the largest file first ln link a file pwd Print Working Directory cd Change Directory (eg. cd /tmp/var) mkdir Make Directory mkdir -p parent/{F1,F2,F3}/{temp1,temp2} creates folder “Parent” with sub-directories F1, F2 & F3 each, with temp1 & temp2 directores inside each sub-directory. rm or rmdir Remove Directory, mv or mvdir (eg. mvdir folder /new/dir) Options: -r or -R “Recursive”, applies command throughout eg. rm -r foldername removes folder & it’s contents .. Parent Directory (One level above), // Root directory touch Create new file (eg. touch dir/sample.txt) cp Copy (eg. cp test.txt dir/test2.txt copies test.txt to directory dir and renames it test2.txt) rm to remove file shred to permanently delete file * Wildcard eg. rm test/*-geoff removes all files in directory test that end in “-geoff” eg. rm * will remove all files in the current directory && Execute another command in the same line ONLY if the previous command worked
| Pipe, Redirects command into another (from left to right)
|| Double Pipe, operates as command 1 OR command 2
; Semicolon, starts an entirely new command regardless of what was before
Writing/Finding Data > Create/write to file (eg. echo “Hello world” > Hi.txt creates Hi.txt with “Hello world” inside) >> Append to file (Creates file if it doesn’t exist, adds to existing file if it does) cat Concatenate (combine & display)
Options: -s suppress repeated empty output lines, -n display line numbers, -e $ at end of line, -b # of non-empty lines eg. cat 1.txt 2.txt combines files & displays on console eg. cat 1.txt 2.txt **\>** 1\_2.txt combines & writes data to 1_2.txt (overwrites if 1_2.txt already exists) eg. cat 1.txt 2.txt **\>>** 1\_2.txt combines & writes data to 1_2.txt (appends if 1_2.txt already exists) more Display file one page at a time, spacebar for next page. less Greater flexibility. Scroll horizontally/forward/backward one line at a time q to exit file line display head Display top 10 lines (eg. head -n 4 logfile1.txt displays first 4 lines with line #’s) tail Display bottom 10 lines (eg. tail -26 test.rtf shows last 26 lines of test.rtf) cmp Compare files diff Show differences between files sed Edits a stream sed s/(old value)/(replacement value)/ [CAUTION: sed overwrites] eg. “The Dog chased a Ball”, sed s/Ball/Cat/ changes it to “The Dog chased a Cat” awk Data processing and extracting/reporting from streams [Using awk] eg. awk -F, '{print $(field#)}' then awk isolates column (field#) with ‘,’ separating data eg. awk -F ‘{print $4, $7}’ reads a new column for each space, prints columns 4 & 7 find Searches for file/directory names [Using find function] Options: iname ignores case, -type file (f) or directory (d), eg. find -type f -iname *.txt’ finds all .txt files eg. find -type d -iname rogers/* finds directories starting with “rogers” ignoring case eg. find /directory/folder -type f -iname /log.txt searches different directory whereis all locations of a file grep Searches inside files for a string [Using Grep] Options: -c count, -r recursive, -i case insensitive, -l list filename eg. grep bob log1.txt finds ‘bob’ in log1.txt eg. grep -i bob log1.txt find ‘bob’ regardless of casing eg. grep -il bob \*.txt finds ‘bob’ in all text files, but only returns filenames xxd Provides a Hex dump for a file Networking wget Download a file from a URL
Options: ‐‐output-document=filename.html example.com (Rename file being downloaded), Download to specific folder: ‐‐directory-prefix=folder/subfolder example.com Resume interrupted download: ‐‐continue example.com/big.file.iso Download IF server has a newer version:‐‐continue ‐‐timestamping wordpress.org/latest.zip Download from multiple URLs listed in txt file: ‐‐input list-of-file-urls.txt Download sequentially numbered files: http://example/{1..20}.jpg Download an entire webpage wget ‐‐page-requisites ‐‐span-hosts ‐‐convert-links ‐‐adjust-extension http://example.com/dir/file curl Call a URL Options: --abstract-unix-socket <path> Connect via abstract Unix domain socket -a, --append Append to target file when uploading -E, --cert <certificate[:password]> Client certificate file and password -K, --config <file> Read config from a file -b, --cookie <data|filename> Send cookies from string/file -c, --cookie-jar <filename> Write cookies to filename after operation -d, --data <data> HTTP POST data -G, --get Put the post data in the URL and use GET -x, --proxy [protocol://]host[:port] Use this proxy -U, --proxy-user <user:password> Proxy user and password --pubkey <key> SSH Public key file name -u, --user <user:password> Server user and password ping Sends Ping Options: ping -c 5 Sends 5 pings netstat Shows open ports uname OS & system hardware info Options: a (--all) All system info, -n (-- nodename) System network name -r (--kernal-release) Kernel release -v (--kernal-version) Kernel version -s (--kernal-name) Kernel name -m (--machine) Hardware name -p (--processor) Processor architecture -i (--hardware-platform) Hardware platform -o (--operating-system) Operating system nslookup Lookup DNS Records Options: -type=(any, soa, ns, a, mx, txt) Displays DNS record type Archive & Compress Tar: tar [option(s)] [archive_name.tar] [objects_to_archive]
Full tar options list tar {A|c|d|r|t|u|x}[GnSkUWOmpsMBiajJzZhPlRvwo] Options c create archive (also --create) -z Creates compressed gzip archive (title ends in “.tar.gz” or “.tgz”) -j Creates compressed bzip archive (title ends in “.tar.bz2” or “.tbz” --exclude Excludes files and folders in archived directory f file, must be last option & followed by archive title. (also --file) x extract archive (also --extract, --get) [must use -z or -j if archive is compressed] -C Extracts archive to different directory (directory path must follow) -k keeps existing files when extracting. (also –keep-old-files) --wildcards “*.jpg”: Extracts files ending in .jpg (works for any) --keep-newer-files Don’t replace existing files newer than archive --keep-directory-symlink Don’t replace symlinks --no-overwrite-dir Preserve metadata --overwrite Overwrite existing files --overwrite-dir Overwrite metadata --recursive-unlink Remove all files in directory before extraction --remove-files Remove files from disk after adding to archive --skip-old-files Don’t replace existing files when extracting, skip over -U Remove each file prior to extracting over (also --unlink-first) -W Verify archive (also --verify) -v verbose, displays archive results -vv very verbose, displays detailed results including file paths & permissions -r append (also --append) tar rf archive.tar archive/ folder/ file.txt adds folder & file.txt to archive.tar -u update, just archiving files (also –update) -t list archive contents (also --list) tar tvf archive.tar List contents of “archive.tar” with verbose output -d difference, comparing archive & file system. (also -diff, --compare) --delete delete from archive, does not operate on compressed archives. -A Apprend archive to another, must be same format. (also catenate, --concatenate) --test-label Test archive volume label, codes as 0 if match found, codes 1 if not. Zip/Unzip
Leaves behind original and creates new zip files zip command format is: zip [option(s)] [archive_name.zip] [objects_to_archive] tar -jxvf archive.tar.bz2 extracts the .bz2 “archive.tar” with verbose output Options: -[0-9]: Level of compression, -0 is none & -9 is maximum -e Adds password protection (use this and not -P) unzip command format is: unzip [option(s)] [archive_name.zip] -v verbose -l list files -t test files to be unzipped gzip/gunzip gzip creates new gzip file and removes original (default) Format: gzip [option(s)] [archive_name.zip] Options -c: Leaves original file [output needs to be redirected] (also --stdout, --to-stdout) > to output to filename.type.gz -r Recursive compression down sub-directories -[0-9] Level of compression, -0 is none & -9 is maximum gunzip short options (also “gzip -d” to “decompress”) -t test files to be gunzipped (silent if no issue) tar -tzf my_tar.tar.gz >/dev/null tests & throws away output without unzipping bzip2/bunzip2 Very similar to gzip (greater compression), uses most of the same commands but with b_2 Scripting Bash Scripting Cheatsheet Full BASH Scripting Reference
BASH Options list Bash Shell Scripting [Full Book] Common Newbie Bash Mistakes ./script.sh will run script.sh chmod +x script.sh will compile the changes made after editing script.sh nano Command line text editor (vim is also available) nano index.html will open the index.html file for editing If the file does not already exist, nano/vim will create it CtrlS saves the file, and CrtlX exits the editor User, Group & System Management Linux Handbook [Huge Free Resource] Important Linux Directories and their structure {#important-linux-directories-and-their-structure}
Important folders in /etc /etc/passwd - used to keep track of every registered user that has access to a system List all usernames - less /etc/passwd or awk -F: '{ print $1}' /etc/passwd /etc/group - used to keep track of every registered group that has access to a system /etc/groups - does not exist /etc/shadow - system file storing encrypted user passwords (accessible only to root) sudo
sudo su Switch to root user sudo -l List sudo permissions of current user sudo -lU :user List sudo permissions of <user> sudo visudo Allows safe editing of the ‘sudoers’ file User & Group management
chmod, chgrp, groupadd, usermod -g,
Chgrp and Sharing Linux Directories
groups <user> List groups user is in id <user> Same as above but with GIDs sudo adduser <user> Add user to system sudo deluser <user> Delete user from system sudo addgroup <group> Add group to system sudo delgroup <group> Delete group from system sudo usermod -aG <user><group> - adds user to group sudo usermod -G <user><group> - add user to group exclusively (no other groups) sudo usermod -L <user> Lock user from accessing system chown
Command Format is: sudo chown <owner>:<group> <item>
sudo chown root test.txt change owner of test.txt to user root sudo chown :root test change owner of test to group root sudo chown -R mike:sally test change owner test to user mike and group sally chmod
Command Format is: sudo chmod <command> file
sudo chmod 755 foo.txt adds read, write, execute to foo.txt for owner; read and execute for groups and others sudo chmod +x foo.txt adds execute access to foo.txt for all users sudo chmod -x foo.txt removes execute access to foo.txt for all users sudo chmod u-w foo.txt removes write access to foo.txt for all users sudo chmod g=rx,o= foo.txt give group read & execute access to foo.txt; no access for others sudo chmod u=rw,g=rw,o=w foo.txt read/write for owner & group, write only for others sudo chmod u=rwx,g-r,u+r foo.txt read/write/execute for user to foo.txt, remove read for group, add read for others System Management
apt-get Package Management

content:
Network security is the practices and policies used to protect and monitor a computer network’s resources against threats and risks.
Client-server model is a network computing model that defines how resources and services are shared across a network. Uses a “request and response” method of device communication.
Network threats and risks
Unauthorized access into networks Denial of service (DoS) attacks Eavesdropping Data modification (eg attacker steals your data & modifies without your knowledge) Local Area Network (LAN) is a private computer network that connects devices in smaller physical areas like a room or single building, such as a small office or home network.
Advantages: Network speed/performance, security, versatility Disadvantages: Limited to only sharing within their own network Wide Area Network (WAN) is a network used to connect multiple LANs (Internet is a WAN)
Disadvantages: Security Issues, Troubleshooting is challenging Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) Model Mnemonic: “Please do not throw sausage pizza away” Layer 1 - Physical: Cables & Hubs. Pinouts, Cable Specs, Network Interface Cards Layer 2 - Data Link: Ethernet. Uses frames, MAC address Layer 3 - Network: IP Address. Uses packets, Transfer address to physical, network routing Layer 4 - Transport: TCP, UDP. Split communication into packages Layer 5 - Session: Traffic Control. Establish, Manage, Terminate, Coordinate comms Layer 6 - Presentation: **Format Data (ASCII, jpg, ect). Encryption/Decryption Layer 7 - Application: End User. Data Presentation. Enables Apps to access the net (SMTP, HTTP, FTP)
Network Devices Router Used to connect two different LANS, two different WANs, or a LAN to a WAN Switch Forwards resources within a network (connects devices within a LAN)
Typically in large businesses with many computers Typically feed into routers and can be programmed for resource management Bridge Same as switch but only two connections, often used to tie two LANs together Hub (OUTDATED) Same as a switch but cannot be programmed Network Interface Controller (NIC) Connects Computer to a network Usually a circuit board or a chip Each computer must have a NIC to receive/send resources Modem (Modulator-DeModulator) Converts data to a format for the network Computer speaks digital, ISP speaks analog Wireless Access Point (WAP) Provides wireless devices network connectivity All-in-One Devices Integrate Modems, WAPs, routers, and more. Advantages: Easy to use, less equipment to setup/maintain Disadvantages: Single point of failure, difficult to troubleshoot. Network Security Devices Firewall Monitors & manage incoming/outgoing traffic
Typically placed right at LAN entry point to protect confidentiality & integrity Load Balancers Distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers Ensures no single server has too much traffic, protecting resource availability Typically placed right after the firewall Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) Smaller subnetwork within a LAN to protect internal data Typically has it’s own network security devices to detect/block before reaching internal networks Network Topology Linear Each device is connected to the next via two-way link
Advantages: Adding devices to the network is easy. Disadvantages: Single device failure can interrupt entire network. Variable latency between devices Ring Each device is connected to the next in the loop (uni or bi-directional) Advantages: Simple, no central node, adding is easy Disadvantages: Every device is a failure point, variable latency Star Each device is attached to a central node (eg. a server) Advantages: Consistent latency, easy to extend, node failure has no effect on network Disadvantages: Network size limited by central node connections, difficult if central node is far from end devices Bus Each device is attached to a central data link Advantages: Fast transmission, easy to expand Disadvantages: Bandwidth waste, devices cannot transmit simultaneously Tree Each device has only one connection between any only connected Advantages: Easy to expand Disadvantages: If a node fails all devices below are effected Fully Connected Every device is connected to every other device Advantages: High redundancy, fast transmission Disadvantages: Complicated setup/management, expensive to establish Calculating the number of wires for a fully meshed network Mesh Many (but not all) devices are connected to find shortest path to forward data Advantages/Disadvantages: Same as fully connected Hybrid Mixture of different network topologies Advantages/Disadvantages: Depend on network types being combined IP Addresses Internet Protocol (IP) is a numerical network address associated with a device such as a computer, printer, router or server.
www.whatsmyip.org iplocation.io [Significant info from multiple sources, inc geolocation & ASN] Binary to IP Converter (for IPv4) IP Types IPv4 Four Octets (8 binary bits = one byte) ranging 0-255, separated by decimals (eg. 10.4.79.254) IPv6 Eight groups of 2 bytes encoded in hexidecimal (hex) separated by colon (eg. 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334)
IPv6 has not been widely adopted and many devices need to be updated before accepting IPv6 addresses IP Categories Private IP addresses are NOT exposed to the internet (typically within a LAN)
Assigned by LAN’s network administrator Can be reused, won’t conflict across different networks, more secure Private IPv4 ranges fall within: Class A Private = 10.0.0.0 - 10.255.255.255 (16,777,216 available) Class B APIPA = 169.254.0.0 - 169.254.255.255 Microsoft Windows feature automatically assigns this range if a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) server is not available Class B Private = 172.16.0.0 - 172.31.255.255 (1,048,576 available) Class C Private = 192.168.0.0 - 192.168.255.255	(65,536 available) Public IP addresses can be accessed over the internet Assigned in IP ranges by an Internet Service Provider (ISP) Any address not within the Private IP4 ranges is public Public IPv4 can also be classed: Class A (Large Org) = 1.0.0.0 - 127.0.0.0 (1oct = 1-127) Class B (Medium Org) = 128.0.0.0 - 191.0.0.0 (1oct = 128-191) Class C (Small LAN) = 192.0.0.0 - 223.255.255.0 (1oct = 192-223) Class D (Multicasting)	= 224.0.0.0 - 239.255.255.255 (1oct = 224-239) Class E (Research) = 240.0.0.0 - 255.255.255.255 (1oct = 240-255) Loop-back addresses are for network testing Range 127.0.0.1 - 127.255.255.255 These are virtual IP addresses that cannot be assigned to a device, but are used to ping a computer’s TCP/IP network software driver Subnetting Subnetting is the process of breaking up an IP address range into smaller, more specific networks of grouped devices.
IPv4 Subnet Calculator IPv6 Subnet Calculator Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) is a format fixing the number of bits which are static for the network. CIDR-IP Range Calculator
CIDR replaces the older A, B and C classes of IP addresses 0 & 255 are reserved for the subnet ID and broadcasting respectively Example: 192.243.3.0 /24 = 24 bits of the address (eg. 1st 3 octets) are static, so 192.243.3 are fixed and up to 255 IP addresses are available with the final octet MAC Address Media Access Control (MAC) Addresses are burned-in addresses assigned to network interface cards which must be unique to each NIC on the same network.
MAC addresses have 6 sets of alphanumeric characters separated by colons First 24-bits (1st 3 octets) identify the device vendor/manufacturer Example: 00:0a:95:9d:68:16 where 00:0a:95 is Apple, Inc. MAC Address Lookup Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) maps the MAC address to an IP address within a LAN
ARP cache poisoning or ARP spoofing is a MitM attack that allows attackers to intercept communication between network devices. ARP Spoofing Explainer(https://www.imperva.com/learn/application-security/arp-spoofing/) DNS Domain Name System (DNS) translates domain names to IP addresses, eg. facebook.com translates to the IP address 31.13.65.36
Cisco DNS Best Practice, Network Protections, and Attack Identification DNS Records Explained (A, AAAA, CNAME, DNAME, MX, NS, PTR, SPF, ect) DNS Lookup directs the browser to search a series of caches to find the IP address associated with the domain name. This search process is; Browser cache Operating System cache (stored in hosts file) Internet Service Provider (ISP) cache Top-Level Domain (TLD) cache Reverse DNS Lookup provides the domain name for a given IP address, and is stored as a PTR (Pointer) record on the special .arpa domain name.
Reverse DNS Lookup IPv4 “A” records are stored under the subdomain_ .in-addr.arpa IPv6 “AAAA” records are stored under the subdomain .ip6.arpa DNS hijacking Type of network attack that exploits DNS vulnerabilities to divert web traffic away from legitimate servers and to fake/malicious servers. Uniform Resource Locatior (URL) is the specific location of a resource in a domain
Syntax: [URI scheme]://[subdomain].[domain].[TLD][/path/][filename] Example: https://www.facebook.com/photos/catpicture.jpg https_ = Uniform Resource Identifer for “Secure Hypertext Transfer Protocol” www = subdomain facebook = primary domain .com = Top-Level Domain /photos/ = path where the resource is located catpicture.jpg_ = resource being requested Network Protocols Network Protocols ensure messages are fully sent and understood.
Example: FIN is used by TCP messages to indicate the end of a message Common Protocols HTTP: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (Web traffic) FTP: File Transfer Protocol (File transfer) [INSECURE] PAP: Password Authentication Protocol (User authentication) SMB: Server Message Block (Windows file sharing) NetBIOS: Network Basic Input/Output System (LAN communication) Network Packet is a binary message adhering to protocol rules. Example IPv4 is up to 65,535 bytes including Header (20-60 bytes) + Payload Headers may contain protocol name/version, destination address, packet length Version is defined Transmission Control Protocol requires acknowledgement to ensure all data is transmitted without error and in the correct order.
TCP three-way handshake is the process of establishing a reliable connection to transmit data between devices. Setup = SYN → | SYN-ACK ← | ACK → (then data →) Terminate = FIN → | ACK ← FIN ← | ACK → User Datagram Protocol (UDP) is useful for situations when it’s not necessary for all data to reach the destination.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) is a protocol used for automatically setting different configurations (including IP-addresses).
DHCP Four-way handshake: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge DHCP Starvation is a type of DDos attack where a DHCP Server is flooded with Discover requests, and the DHCP server runs out of internal IP addresses to assign to legitimate users. DHCP Spoofing can follow DHCP Starvation in order to provide a false DHCP server to allocate IP addresses to create a Man-In-The-Middle situation Network Address Translation (NAT) is a method of mapping a private IP address to a public IP address and vice versa. Routing is the act of choosing the path that traffic takes in or across networks.
Unicast: A single device delivers a message to another single, specific device. Broadcast: A single device broadcasts a message to all devices on that network. Multicast: A device sends a message to devices that have expressed interest in receiving the message. Routing can also be either static or dynamic
Static routing is the manual configuration of a network route, typically done by a network administrator. Advantages: Lower router CPU, admin has full control of routing behavior. Disadvantages: Fault tolerance, meaning if a device on a manually created path fails, the route can’t be adjusted. Dynamic Routing Types of Routing Protocols [Comprehensive] Ports Ports are access points for transmitting and receiving data Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) is the entity officially responsible for assigning port numbers for a designated purpose. Port Numbers range from 0 to 65535
System ports (0-1023) Restricted to the OS or administrator Well-Known Ports: 20 (FTP - Transfer) 21 (FTP - Commands) 22 (SSH) 23 (TELNET) 25 (SMTP) 53 (DNS) 67 (DHCP - Data to Server) 68 (DHCP Data to Client) 80 (HTTP) 81 (TorPark) 88 (Kerberos Authenticate) 109 (POP2) 110 (POP3) 123 (NTP) 143 (IMAP) 264 (BGMP) 443 (HTTPS) 464 (Kerberos Change/Set Password) 543 (Kerberos login) 545 (Kerberos Remore Shell) 546 (DHCPv6 Client) 565 (DHCPv6 server) Registered/User ports (1024-49151) Normal users launching services 3389 (RDP) 8005 (Tomcat Remote Shutdown) 8333 (Bitcoin) Dynamic/Private ports (49152-65535) “Source” ports for machine→machine Network Tools Nmap - IP address & Port scanner
Nmap Cheat Sheet Wireshark Wireshark User Manual Wireshark Learning Resources General Wireshark Filters Wireshark MAN Page Wireshark Filters (WifiNinjas Blog) Wireshark Cheat Sheet [Important Cheat Sheet] frame contains “string” Searches all frames for a specific string frame.number in {frame#, frame#…} Displays the frames listed
UFW ufw version Determine what version of UFW is installed. sudo ufw reset Reset all UFW rules to factory defaults. sudo ufw status Check the current status of the firewall. sudo ufw enable Start the firewall and update rules. sudo ufw default deny incoming Block all incoming connections. sudo ufw default allow outgoing Allow all outgoing connections. sudo ufw allow Open specific ports (eg. 80, 22, 443) sudo ufw deny Close specific ports. sudo ufw delete Delete rules. sudo ufw disable Shut down the firewall. sudo ufw reload Reload the UFW firewall. sudo apt remove ufw Uninstall ufw Firewalld sudo /etc/init.d/firewalld start start firewalld. sudo service firewalld stop stop firewalld sudo service firewalld status firewalld status sudo firewall-cmd --list-all-zones list all current zones. sudo firewall-cmd --zone=home --change-interface=eth0 bind together interfaces. sudo firewall-cmd --get-services list currently configured services. sudo firewall-cmd --zone=home --list-all list all currently configured services for a specific zone. sudo firewall-cmd --zone=home --add-rich-rule= add specific rules to specific zones Network security monitoring Uses a variety of data analysis tools to detect and stop threats after most front-end layers are compromised.
SIEM and SOAR ELK Stack Elasticsearch - Storage engine for storing and indexing data Logstash - Log aggregator Kibana - Visualisation Splunk Splunk Quick Reference Guide Splunk Fundamentals 1,2,3 Snort (NIDS) Snort uses rules to detect and prevent intrusions. Snort operates by:
Reading a configuration file. Loading the rules and plugins. Capturing packets and monitoring traffic for patterns specified in the loaded rules. When traffic matches a rule pattern, generating an alert and/or logging the matching packet for later inspection. Rules can direct Snort to monitor the following information:
OSI layer: Watches for IP vs. TCP data. Source and destination address: Where the traffic is flowing from and to. Byte sequences: Patterns contained in data packets that might indicate malware, etc. Consider the following Snort rule:
alert ip any any -> any any {msg: “IP Packet Detected”;} This rule logs the message “IP Packet Detected” whenever it detects an IP packet. Example: alert tcp any 21 -> 10.199.12.8 any {msg: "TCP Packet Detected";}
This rules triggers an alert whenever a TCP packet from port 21, with any source IP address, is sent to the IP 10.199.12.8. With each alert, it will print the message “TCP Packet Detected.” \
Rule Header
alert: The action that Snort will take when triggered. tcp: Applies the rule to all TCP packets. any: Applies the rule to packets coming from any source IP address. 21: Applies the rule to packets from port 21. ->: Indicates the direction of traffic. 10.199.12.8: Applies the rule to any packet with this destination IP address. any: Applies the rule to traffic to any destination port. Rule Option
{msg: "TCP Packet Detected";} The message printed with the alert. Snort provides many additional actions and protocols, which can be combined to design rules for almost any type of packet.

Christmas Island is listed under Oceania in Cave Regions.
Cave Regions No local cave regions listed yet. Caves & Dive Sites See the linked cave regions above. Backlinks Cave Regions Diving Existing Notes About Go in dry season: May to November
Red crab migration: Oct to December Whale Sharks: November to January Speak to Kat (Matt’s partner) - look at her PhD research Caves Whip Cave? Runaway Cave?
Lost Lake Cave Location: Western plateau, inland from Flying Fish Cove Type: Partially flooded limestone cave Details: Known to contain an underground lake with significant depth. The full extent of the submerged section has never been explored, but it is considered one of the most promising inland sites for potential cave diving. Exploration Status: Dry portions mapped; no documented dive attempts. Daniel Roux Cave Location: Near the eastern coast, northeast of South Point Type: Dry limestone cave with multiple chambers Details: While primarily dry, reports mention water seepage and active flow in the wet season. Potential exists for deeper sections to be partially flooded. Exploration Status: Surveyed, but no recorded underwater exploration. The Dales Location: Western coast, near Hugh’s Dale Waterfall Type: Karst spring and stream system Details: Features spring-fed water emerging from the base of limestone cliffs. The area around Hugh’s Dale and Anderson Dale may be connected to subterranean water systems—possible resurgence cave diving target. Exploration Status: Surface features documented; no known underwater exploration. Hosnies Spring Cave Location: North coast, near Hosnies Spring Type: Coastal karst feature with permanent spring Details: This area features a freshwater spring discharging into a brackish mangrove environment, suggesting a potential coastal cave system or resurgence beneath. Exploration Status: Caves reported nearby but not explored underwater. Waterfall Cave / Runoff Sites (Unnamed) Location: North-west coast cliffs between Martin Point and Ethel Beach Type: Sea caves and freshwater outflows Details: Rainfall channels sometimes discharge clear freshwater through cliffs, indicating potential connections to karst drainage systems that could be explored from the sea side via cave diving. Exploration Status: Not documented or surveyed for cave access, but satellite imagery shows several sea-level notches. Dolly Beach & Greta Beach Karst System Location: South-east coast Type: Cliff-edge karst with marine influence Details: Both beaches are bordered by steep limestone with visible dissolution features. No documented caves, but the geological setting is favourable for sea cave development, possibly with partially submerged access. Exploration Status: No known surveys, but suitable for scouting. Trips References Satellite Imagery & Karst Mapping Christmas Island’s unique karst topography is well-documented and can be explored through various resources:
Geoscience Australia: Offers detailed topographic and geological maps, including the 1:30,000 scale map that highlights karst features and cave locations. ga.gov.au NASA Worldview: Provides high-resolution satellite imagery, allowing you to examine surface features and terrain. ga.gov.au+5earth.google.com+5zoom.earth+5 Zoom Earth: Features daily updated satellite images, useful for observing current conditions and planning field activities. zoom.earth+1worldview.earthdata.nasa.gov+1 Google Earth: Utilize the 3D terrain feature to identify potential cave entrances and understand the island’s topography. Several expeditions have explored Christmas Island’s caves, providing valuable insights:
2013 National Geographic Expedition: advanceddivermagazine.com+1youtube.com+1 (March 2013, with Wet mules) Western Australian Speleological Group (WASG): wasg.org.au) (October 2023) Helictite Journal: Ken Grimes’ publication, “Karst Features of Christmas Island,” helictite.caves.org.au

Certified Information Systems Auditor Focus: Specialises in information systems auditing—planning and performing audits, evaluating governance and controls, and reporting assurance over IT-enabled business processes and information assets. (ISACA)
Industry: Suits organisations with strong assurance and compliance needs such as government, critical infrastructure, finance, healthcare, large enterprises, and consulting/audit firms. (ISACA)
Requirements Pass the CISA Exam (US$575 ISACA Member, US$760 Non-member) Format: 150 multiple-choice questions, scaled score of 450 or higher (on a 200–800 scale) to pass. Duration: 4 hours. Content: Information System Auditing Process (18%) Governance & Management of IT (18%) Information Systems Acquisition, Development & Implementation (12%) Information Systems Operations and Business Resilience (26%) Protection of Information Assets (26%) Relevant work experience At least five years of professional work experience in information systems auditing, control, assurance, or security. Experience must be within the 10 years preceding the application date, and you must have experience in at least 1 of the 5 CISA job practice domains. You have five years after passing the exam to apply for certification. Experience waivers can reduce the required five years by up to a maximum of three years (for example, via combinations of general IS/audit experience and education waivers). Submit the certification application and pay the US$50 application processing fee. Agree to ISACA’s Code of Professional Ethics and ongoing continuing professional education requirements. Domain 1A - Information Systems Auditing Process Planning The IS Auditor’s Role
Strategic partner to the enterprise Core Mission: *Evaluate and improve risk management, control and governance processes Auditor’s Mindset Objectivity & Independence Focus on Business Risk & Value Systematic & Disciplined Approach 1 - IS Audit Standards, Guidelines, and Codes of Ethics Planning is Paramount Ensures audit efficiency & effectiveness Directs resources to areas of greatest risk Maximises the value and impact of the audit Cost of Poor Planning Wasted resources & time Overlooked critical risks Audit that fails to provide meaningful assurance Is Audit Standards, Guidelines and Code of Ethics Key Framework: ISACA’s IT Assurance Framework (ITAF) Purpose: Ensure consistency, quality and professionalism in IS auiting Exam Tip: Adherence to ISACA Standards is mandatory for CISA holders
Audit Charter - Authority to Audit Purpose: Outlines overall authority, scope, and responsibilities of the audit function Content: Describes the mission, independence, and access rights of the audit team Approval: Must be approved by the highest level of governance (eg. Audit Committee, Board of Directors, or senior management) Exam Tip: Audit Charter is the foundational document that grants the audit function its power & legitimacy
IT Assurance Framework (ITAF) Hierarchy Standards: Mandatory requirements - minimum level of acceptable performance Guidelines: Non-mandatory (optional) assistance. How to implement the standards Tools & Techniques: Practical “How-To” examples (checklists, audit programs, ect) Exam Tip: You MUST follow Standards. Consider Guidelines but deviate with professional judgement and justification
ITAF Standards Catagories General Standards: The “Who” - Attributes of the auditor and audit function Ethics, independence, competence Performance Standards: The “How” - Define the nature of the audit work itself Planning, Risk assessment, evidence collection Reporting Stanards: The “What” - Define the nature and content of the audit report Communication of results, findings, recommendations ISACA Code of Professional Ethics Non-negotiable requirement for all CISA holders Functions as a primary administrative control for the profession Mitigates the risk of audit failure and protects the profession’s reputation Key Principles Support standards Objectivity & Due Care Serve Stakeholders Lawfully Maintain Confidentiality Maintain Competency Informal Appropriate Parties Support Professional Education Failure to comply can result in an investigation and disciplinary measures Sanctions include remrimand, suspension, revocation of certification Exam Tip: Code of Ethics has real teeth, not just a guideline
Management of the IS Audit Function Leadership: The IS audit function must be managed to fulfill its objectives while preserving independence and competence Resource Management Staffing - Auditors must maintain competency through continuous training on new technologies and audit techniques Tools: Management must provide necessary resources like Computer-Assisted Audit Techniques (CAATs) for specialised audits Using Experts: Auditors may engage external experts for highly specialised areas Responsibility: Auditor must assess the experts competence and independence and supervise their work Ultimate liability for the audit opinion is NOT delegated - auditor is accountable 2 - Types of Audits, Assessments, and Reviews Assurance The level of confidence and trust that an organisation’s systems, processes, and controls are effective in protecting information assets, managing risks, and ensuring compliance with relevant standards and policies. Who, how and what of an audit affects confidence Selecting the Right Lens Audits: Highest assurance with formal opinion against established criteria Assessments: Less formal, internal focus on identifying risks and gaps Reviews: Limited assurance with less extensive testing than a full audit Exam Tip: The choice depends on the level of assurance required by stakeholders
Taxonomy of Audit Engagements Compliance Audit: Adherence to laws, regulations, policies (GDPR, PCI DSS) Financial Audit: Accuracy of financial reporting and the supporting IT controls Operational Audit: Efficiency and effectiveness of operations Integrated Audit: Combines Financial and IS/Operational audit objectives (Sarbane-Oxley “SOX” requirement) IS Audit: Focus on CIA triad of information assets Third-Party Service Audit: Audits outsourced processes, resulting in a service auditors report (SOC report) that the organisation’s auditor can rely on Computer Forensic Audit: Specialised investigation of electronic devices to gather and preserve evidence for legal proceedings Functional Audit: Independent evaluation of a software product to verify that it’s functionality and performance meet specified requirements Readiness Assessment: Review of an organisation’s current state of compliance against a standard, focusing on control design to identify gaps before a formal audit Control Self-Assessment (CSA) A management technique where business units assess their own control environments Purpose Increases control awareness and ownership within the business Identifies risks and control gaps early Serves as a valuable input for the internal audit function Auditor’s Role: Acts as a facilitator for CSA workshops and processes, not as the one performing the assessment 3 - Risk Based Audit Planning Core Principle: Concentrate audit resources on areas that pose the greatest risk to the organisation’s objectives Benefits Efficiency: Avoids wasting time on low-risk areas Effectiveness: Provides the most relevant assurance to leadership Exam Tip: The first step in any risk-based audit is to understand the business
Short Term VS Long-term Audit Planning Short-term (Annual) Planning Considers audit issues to be covered during the current year Forms the basis for the annual audit plan Long-term Planning Considers the strategic changes in the organisation’s IT environment and direction Aligns the audit function with the long-term goals of the business Process: This analysis should occur at least annually and be updated for significant changes (eg. Acquisitions, new regulations) The plan must be approved by the audit committee Effects of Laws and Regulations on Planning Auditor’s Responsibility: Is auditor must identify all applicable laws, regulations, and contractual requirements relevant to the audit Impact on Scope: External requirements that directly impact the audit scope and objectives Audit Steps Identify and document applicable laws and regulations (eg. Data privacy, commerce, industry-specific rules) Assess if management has incorporated these requirements into policies and procedures Review internal documents and controls for adherence Exam Tip: You won’t be asked about specific laws, but you will be tested on how you would audit for compliance with them
Risk-Based Audit Planning Lifecycle Audit Planning Lifecycle Understand the Business: Define the “audit universe” (all potential audit able entities) Perform a Risk Assessment: Identify threats and vulnerabilities, prioritise high-risk areas Identify Existing Controls: What has management done to mitigate the high risks? Determine Residual Risk: How much risk is left after controls are considered? Develop the audit plan: Define scope, objectives, and resources based on residual risk Approved by the audit committee Audit Risk and Materiality Audit Risk: Risk of issuing an incorrect audit opinion (eg. Saying controls are effective when they are not) Materiality: Importance or significance of an item in the context of the enterprise as a whole. An error is material if it could influence the decisions of stakeholders Formula: Audit Risk (AR) = Inherent Risk (IR) x Control Risk (CR) x Detection Risk (DR) Inherent Risk: Risk before control implementation Control Risk: Risk a material error that would not be prevented/detected in a time lying basis by the system of internal controls Detection Risk: Risk that material errors or misstatements will not be detected by an IS auditor Residual Risk: Risk that remains after controls have been implemented Key Relationship: Inverse relationship between materiality and audit risk If an area is highly material (very important) then the acceptable level of audit risk is low, meaning the auditor must perform more rigorous testing 4 - Types of Controls and Considerations What is a Control? A policy, procedure, practice, or organisational structure that provides reasonable assurance that business objectives will be achieved Prevents, detects, or corrects undesirable events Control Objctive: The specific goal a control is designed to achieve COBIT and Others ISACA’s Primary Framework is “COBIT” COBIT: Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies Other Prescriptive Frameworks CIS: Center for Internet Security Controls (Prioritised set of best practices for cyber security) OWASP: Open framework for software security PCI DSS: Requirements for protecting payment card data CSA Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM): Framework for cloud computing security General Controls and Application Controls General Controls (ITGCs): Applies to the entire IT environment (data centers, networks, operating systems, ect) and provides foundation for all overall controlled structure Change management, logical access policies, disaster recovery Application Controls: Specific to particular software application or business process. Ensures data is complete, accurate, and valid as it is processed Classification by Function Preventative: Stops it occurring (eg. firewall, encryption) Detective: Identifies an incident after occurance (eg. System logs, IDS alerts) Corrective: Remediates the impact of an incident (eg. Incident response, backups) Deterrent: Discourages an individual from causing an incident (eg. Warning sings, barriers) Directive: Mandates (directs, steers) desired behaviour (eg. Policies, laws) Compensating: Alternate control when a primary control is not feasible Exam Tip: Preventative controls are the most effective and desirable type
Classification by Implmentation Administrative (Managerial): “Soft controls” focused on people and processes (eg. Policies, procedures, security awareness training) Technical (Logical): Controls implemented in hardware or software (ACLs, encryption, antivirus) Physical: Controls that protect the physical environment (eg. Fences, locks, security guards, fire suppression) Management Control Monitoring What is it? Management’s own process for monitoring the effectiveness of controls, separate from a formal audit Purpose Identifies control deviations in a timely manner Allows management to take proactive corrective action Drives continuous improvement of the security program Auditor’s Role: The IS auditor can review the results of management’s monitoring efforts as part of their evaluation of the control environment CISA Mindset Think the “ISACA Way”: ALWAYS prioritise business risk (over purely technical issues) Auditor’s Role: Provide assurance, not implement controls First Steps is ALWAYS understand the business context Exam Tip: Practice, practice, practice. Use scenario-based questions to master the application of these concepts
