content:
For the last few years I’ve had the idea of not just a bucket list, but a “ridiculous bucket list” - a list of things that seem utterly outrageous and infeasible, but the likes I would embrace in a heartbeat if the opportunity presented. While my bucket list includes things seeing an erupting volcano or joining the mile-high club, my ridiculous bucket list would have things like “Visit the Moon” and “Discover evidence for alien life on Mars”.
For years I’ve used the 101 Things - Complete List list as a guide for an adventurous life, with it providing opportunities to do, see and experience things that I might not have ever considered. Over time that has kind of merged with my Bucket List. But all of these things have grown out of each other, and it’s been a long while since I sat down to put together a list of utterly ridiculous things I’d like to do with my life.
In many ways, I’d really like to sort through and tick off a lot of the things on my 101/Bucket/50 Goals lists first, but that’s not the way my brain works - if anything I want to merge all three and add in some truly insane shit. I want to live an incredibly adventurous life, and these lists help me sort through my priorities and pick out the experiences that will provide me with incredible stories. And stories are what this is all ultimately about - doing incredible things and sharing them with others.
Right now I have too many different boring things pulling me in too many different directions, and I really lack the strong sense of direction that I’ve experienced before while pursuing my bucket list items. Putting together a ridiculous bucket list that pulls all my different lists together and distils them into something that provides purpose and the opportunity for incredible storytelling is what’s most important here.
So with that in mind, go through the remaining 101 Things - To Do and start putting together the mini-essays you’ll need to write Book - 101 Things. Look at your Bucket List and figure out which parts are genuinely important to you - from that, you’ll be able to refine it all into this “Ridiculous Bucket List” you’re thinking of. But above all, it’s vital that you’re writing about all of this, because there’s no point in having these incredible experiences if you can’t share them through storytelling. Ultimately it’s the books you write that will remain when you’re long gone, and they’ll indirectly help people far more than you ever could directly.
This also reminds me of…
Tomorrow’s Mini Essay: Mini Essay - Why you didn’t think you’d make it to 30
References
title: Mini Essay - Ridiculous Bucket List

content:
Surviving any uncomfortable workplace always requires an evil secret plan on your part, and your current situation is no different.
Your secret is that you’re using them as a stepping stone to more suitable work, and as a way to gain useful experience from both a corporate and technical perspective. From a technical perspective you’re now working in threat intelligence for a critical infrastructure organisation, which looks incredible on your resume. Being able to string those things together means you’re well on your way to choosing the kind of work you want in industries that you feel are important.
The corporate experience is just as important though, as you work in a flexible environment but recognise that it’s not for you. Counting out leave is breaking your heart, and knowing that you can’t just up and go is crushing your sense of freedom. You can survive that for awhile knowing that it’s for a purpose, but it will become harder the longer it goes on because you know the purpose of pushing on where you are is to get to the end - to get what you want and leave.
For you, the secret to working where you are for the last 10 months, and what will get you through the final 6, is knowing that this is a massive stepping stone towards the flexibility and income you desire. You’re being sponsored to study the certification (CISSP) which you’ve known for years is the goal, and you’re gaining highly relevant experience in a vital field. The responsibility for fixing issues weighs heavily on you, and when it’s combined with the organisational bureaucracy you witness, the result is soul-crushing. But if you step back from the responsibility and the misguided sense you “need to fix it all” then it’s a very easy job to do, and it supports your end goals.
While work may have been a source of angst and depression for you over the last few months, having made the decision to leave has eased that pressure and allow you to recognise the real secret of working there - this is just a stepping stone to greater things. Finish the next 6 months, and get everything you need in terms of experience and certifications to go so much further.
title: Mini Essay - Secret to dealing with work

content:
Kindle Not Fade Away (Jim Dodge) I have to laugh about this book because it’s on the 101 Things book list, but I accidentally read all of “Not Fade Away” by Ben Torres-Fong (about the early years of Rolling Stone) and didn’t realise I’d read the wrong book until I went to tick it off the list. I enjoyed both, but this one was certainly a lot weirder and more entertaining. It took me awhile to figure out that the journey was just an excuse to meet weird and wonderful characters along the way, but once I recognised that it was easy to settle in and see wherever the author decided to take it. Reading it wasn’t life changing, but it was certainly a fun read.
Walden (Henry Thoreau) Errrgh, this fucking book. I read this back in 2019 after hearing it referenced in the finale of “Parks an Recreation”, and had high hopes it’d be an inspiring and engaging perspective on life among nature, and specifically the dense pine forests and stunning lakes of the US. I forced my way through this book the first time in 2019, finishing it primarily because it was an audio book I could tune in and out of while walking the dog. Having rewatched “Parks and Recs” again recently, I was similarly inspired to pick up Walden again, this time as an ebook… And felt near instant regret. I’m clearly missing the magic that other people find when they read this, but I genuinely can’t tolerate even a few pages of Thoreau’s prose - all I can think whenever I try is how insufferable I’d have found him in person if we ever met.
Audible The Holographic Universe (Michael Talbot) This was the first book I finished in 2025, and I’ll admit my memory of it is already hazy. What I do remember is that I resonated closely with much of what it shared, and it pushed me to look more closely at holographic theory and consider how it might align with the other reading I’d been doing around quantum information theory too. It also reminded me that Gerard T’Hooft - who I knew from his involvement with Mars One - had been one of world leaders in holographic theory, and how it presents a unique and deeply appealing perspective on the nature of the universe. This is certainly a book I should (and want to) read again in 2026.
A Life of Meaning (James Hollins) This is another book that I read early in the year and don’t have clear memories of. I do know that I enjoyed it, and it felt like quite a gentle read - there wasn’t anything groundbreaking in it for me, but it wasn’t in any way boring or pandering. Like the Holographic Universe, this is something I should probably read again in 2026.
Being Ram Dass (Ram Dass) My first introduction to Ram Dass was through “The Midnight Gospel” on Netflix, with the classic “Just Be Here Now” quote ending the series. I’ve been intrigued for awhile by Alan Watts, and I felt a similar strain of impish spiritualism while listening to Ram Dass’s lectures in “Becoming Nobody” last year, so I picked up “Being Ram Dass” as a way to learn more about Richard Alprin and later Ram Dass. Understanding the journey he took and the person he evolved into as he delvd deeper into love was fascinating, and in many ways this book was more important to read and understand than just his lectures in “Becoming Nobody”. His book “Be Here Now” is in my kindle too, and I expect that it’ll be one of the first things I read in 2026 once I’ve finished the books left from 101 Things - To Do.
Showing Up (Nedd Brockmann) All I can say about this and Nedd Brockmann is what an absolute legend. Some people know they love pushing themselves to do remarkable things, and then there are folks like Nedd who go out and do remarkable things over and over and over again. Not only does Nedd share what it was like to run such epic distances day-in and day-out, but it’s clear throughout the book that he’s just a genuinely good guy who’s doing what he’s doing as a way of supporting a cause he believes in. A genuine pleasure to listen to, and finishing this I felt absolutely inspired to go out and do more remarkable things with my life too.
The Anthropocene Reviewed (John Green) I genuinely don’t remember listening to this. Goodreads tells me I rated it 4 stars, and I remember being excited to read something from John Green who I’d first seen a quote from through Zen Pencils. But I just don’t remember anything from this. Maybe I should relisten to it in 2026, but my gut tells me I wouldn’t get a lot out of it from a 2nd listen.
Can’t Hurt Me (David Goggins) After the way Nedd Brock man raved about meeting Dave Goggins at the end of his book, I got really excited and decided to look him up… And realised that “Can’t Hurt Me” was the same book that Auible had been recommending every time I opened it for the previous few months! This couldn’t have been more of a disappointment compared to Nedd’s book though. I have all the respect in the world for what Dave Goggins did getting through some of the toughest military training in the world, but I also really struggled with the knuckle-dragging mentality. He’s an incredible example that we are ALL capable of when we truly commit body and soul, but I also have to wonder what it all proved. I’m glad I read this, but I’m not sure what I learned from it.
Horus Heresy Series - Warhammer 40k There was a brief period at the start of 2025 when I was looking at getting into painting WH40k models again - something I’d done in high-school, but had dropped in uni and hadn’t been in one place long enough to consider again since. The interest soon passed when I remembered how expensive the plastic is (genuinely eye-watering) but I did go through a run of Games Workshop audiobooks from the Warhammer 40k universe, starting with the Horus Heresy trilogy (“Horus Rising”, “False Gods”, and “Galaxy in Flames”). Some of this was really well written sci-fi, some of it was a bit average, but all of it was interesting from a lore perspective. Having never really understood the WH40k universe, it was interesting to start from the point where it all went wrong (and got interesting) with the fall of Warmaster Horus and the corruption of half the space marine chapters. My limited interest in the boardgames was always massively overshadowed by the lore, and these three books broke down the heart of why the imperium of man looked the way it does in the year 40,000. That said, there were always more interesting parts of the space Marines than the core loyalist chapters and those that turned to chaos, and I realise not that I have always been most intrigued by the edge cases, which explains why I finished this trilogy and moved onto books focused on Alpha Legion and the Dark Angels
Legion (Dan Abnett) - Warhammer 40k This was honestly one of the best books I read out of the entire “Black Library”. Dan Abnett is undoubtably one of the best writers Games Workshop works with, and Alpha Legion are easily one of the most intriguing (chaos?) space marine chapters around. This reads as much like sci-fi as it does a spy novel, and is one of the few WH40k books that I’d recommend as a complete stand-alone or to someone who doesn’t know anything about the universe.
Dark Angels Series - Warhammer 40k Right from the time I first started getting interested in Warhammer in high school, the Dark Angels were what hooked me… And it was honestly just the green colour scheme. Like Alpha legion though, I was lucky that my interest was tied to a chapter that had such a rich and fascinating lore. In high school I only got exposed to that via the 4th edition Dark Angels Codex, but 2025 was the year I discovered that there was an extensive collection of well-made Dark Angel audiobooks on Audbile that covered the history of Caliban before the Lion El Johnson even arrived, all the way through to the total destruction of the planet itself. “Descent of Angels”, “Fallen Angels” and “Angels of Caliban” kind of blend together now that I look back on them, but none of them were disappointing - the whole lore around the corruption of the planet, the betrayal of the Fallen, and the shame that the chapter carries all make for exceptional reading. While I wouldn’t go back to read the Horus Heresy again, I’d be more than temoted to revisit these three.
A Thousand Sons - Graham McNeill I don’t get why the Thousand Sons interested me in WH40k. They’re fully fledged chaos marines, use spells, have a weird Ancient Egyptian vibe and are relatively fragile in-game - all things I wanted to avoid. And yet their lore has always fascinated me, and so I found myself listening to the book dedicated to their Horus Heresy era turn to chaos. It’s a sign of a good Warhammer 40k book when you know how it all ends, but you’re still hoping the kind-of bad guys don’t get absolutely annihilated by the dickish “good guys” (the Space Wolves).
The Master of Mankind - Aaron Dembski-Bowden After all the talk about the Emperor throughout all the Horus Heresy era books I’d read, I figured I"d jump ahead to the book dedicated to him. Honestly, this guy is pretty scummy, but I guess that’s why he makes a great character. The main thing I remember from reading this was hearing about all the lore from the battle for Terra, when the Emperor was just the leader of some war band killing other war bands in the wasteland of Earth while doing weird genetic experiments with his own geneseed. What was more interesting than the Emperor himself was the pretorians that were fighting to protect him. Having never heard of them before, it was fascinating to hear the perspective from the characters tasted with protecting the God-Emperor of humanity.
The Teachings of Don Juan - Carlos Castenada Total change of gears from far-future fantasy sci-fi to Carlos Castenada doing peyote in the desert. I’d heard all about the incredible writing of Castenada and even caught the name drop in “Cloud Atlas” when Tom Hanks’ character asks Halle Berry’s if she ever read any of it. I’d assumed that reading this would itself be some sort of perspective-altering experience, but honestly it just reads like some gringo going down to Mexico and doing a bunch of drugs with an old guy who spoke in riddles. I"m sure this was revolutionary when it was published in the 60’s (?) but when Audible recommended the sequel (included for free in my membership) I decided to pass.
The Tao of Pooh - Benjamin Hoff (reread) I first listened to this driving back from a trip to Olwogin cave on the Roe Plains a few years back, and it was exactly what I needed at the time when I was trying to do too many things and (in the words of Pooh) I was being a “Bissy Backson”. Listening to this on the drive back from the Nullarbor felt just as timely, as I’d slipped into my old “Bissy” ways again and had left my job a few weeks earlier so I could put more time and energy into things I actually care about rather than rushing around trying to do everything and please everyone. I haven’t heard particularly good things about the follow up “The Te of Piglet” but I can absolutely endorse the Tao of Pooh as something I’m going to keep coming back to whenever I lose sight of what’s important in life.
You Are Not So Smart - David McRaney This was probably my least favourite read of 2025. I’m not sure what I thought I was getting when I bought a book on psychology that literally talks down to you with its title, but the whole thing felt incredibly condescending from start to finish. Nothing in this felt particularly revolutionary from a psychology perspective, and all of it felt smug and dickish as it built emotional strawmen with hypothetical situations describing how “you” think something might happen, but then says (every fucking chapter) “but you are not so smart” before explaining why you’re a moron for even thinking the way it’s described. Hard pass, 0 stars.
Hour of the Wolf - Blaine Lee Pardoe Much of 2024"s light audiobook listening was consumed with Battletech novels of wildly ranging quality, so when I saw Blaine Lee Pardoe had written another one about the very end of the war for the Inner Sphere with Clan Wolf’s race to claim Terra, then I figured I’d add one more Battletech book to my library. Blaine Lee Pardoe is a bit of a controversial author too given his right-wing Trump-sequel politics (and his history of having some of the characters spout those politics in monologues) but I think he had a very short leash for this novel - given this is book is essentially the end of the Battletech timeline, and the characters in it have been well established in other previous books, there probably wasn’t a lot of room for the Khan of Clan Wolf to suddenly start spouting about libertariaism. But after over 100 Battletech books published through the decades, it was great to read the finale to an extraordinary and fascinating universe.
“Endymion” & “The Rise of Endymion” - Dan Simmons These two books bleed together, but they’re also strangely disconnected from the first two books in the Hyperion saga. If you’ve not read Hyperion, then you absolutely should, but I’m also glad there was a significant gap between my reading of book two (“Fall of Hyperion”) and these books (books three and four). This is twisty, dense and confusing sci-fi at its best, so if you read Hyperion and didn’t like or get it, then don’t push on hoping it gets better - you’ll either like Dan Simmons’ work or you won’t.
“Foundation and Empire” & “Second Foundation” - Isaac Asimov Speaking of twisty, dense and confusing sci-fi, I also finished the Foundation series with these two books. This was definitely spurred on by the excellent TV series, and it was fascinating to read these prior to season three which introduced “The Mule” for the first time. The TV adaptation is excellent given the age of the source material, but that’s not a criticism of these books either - merely that they were certainly written many decades ago, and that occasionally shows in the writing.
Quit - Annie Duke Having never heard of Annie Duke before, I’m not sure why this popped up on my radar to read… other than I was leaving my office job at the same time. Whatever the reason, I’m glad I did - I went into this thinking it’d be a slightly bland take on why people should leave shitty jobs sooner, and certainy wasn’t expecting to hear from a highly-successful professional poker player talking about all the biases humans have towards holding on to everything (jobs, relationships, possessions) for far too long. We invest and then become predisposed to keeping that investment well beyond it’s obvious use-by date, when the logical thing to do is to let go and evolve. I’ll almost certainly reread this in 2026, and hopefully the lessons it provided will sink in a little deeper than they did the first time.
Slow Down - Constance Kassor While “Quit” was a wonderful surprise to read, “Slow Down” felt like a chore. Maybe I came into it with the expectation that it’d provide some insights on how to slow down in life (something I’ve been claiming to want for years now) but what I got was a fairly self-indulgent description of one woman’s year long sabbatical. I kept thinking there’d be some sort of insight or wisdom that’d help others slow down and find a more enjoyable pace in life. But that moment never came, and based on the reviews on Goodreads I’m certainly not the only one who put this book down disappointed.
Blake Crouch Collection: Dark Matter, Recursion, Upgrade - Blake Crouch When I trialled AppleTV, the Dark Matter TV series was one of the first things recommended to me, but I instinctively pushed back against it - I’d signed up for Silo and Foundation, not for some odd split-reality series featuring Joel Edgerton. The audiobook must have popped up on special though, and as soon as I started listening I was hooked. All three books put genuinely edge science (the many-worlds hypothesis, the proposed quantum nature of conciousness, and viral transhumanism) front-and-centre, and push the concepts to the very edge while blending them with insanely-fast action. It’s genuinely hard to keep up with these books, but that challenge is half of the joy - you’re trying to think as hard as the protagonists to figure out the next step. As a trained physicist with an interest in the nature of conciousness, the first two (Dark Matter and Recursion) were easily the most interesting, but Upgrade forced me well outside my comfort zone learning more about human biology than I ever have beforeand. All three books are exceptional, and well worth the effort for anyone interested in modern hard sci-fi… And I did watch (and enjoy) the Dark Matter TV series once I’d finished all three books.
The Dalai Lama’s Cat, Books 4-6 - David Michie I’ve always had a soft spot for David Michie’s books ever since my Mum met him and gave me a paperback version of The Magician of Lhasa. These books are so easy and engaging it’s often easy to mix up which ones you’ve read, which is why I reread For Paws of Spiritual Success before moving onto Awaken the Kitten Within and realising I’d already read that previously too. not that it mattered - it’s a joy to listen to any of these books, and having the author narrate them just adds to the experience. Like the five books before it, Claws of Attraction perfectly wraps a series of core Buddhist tenants in a gentle but engaging story all told through the eyes of “H.H.C” aka “His Holiness’s Cat”. Reading them in order adds a little bit of overall story context, but honestly you could pick any of them up in any order and have a wonderful experience learning a little more about Buddhism from the “most beautiful creature who ever lived”
Altered Carbon Trilogy - Richard K Morgan Netflix’s Altered Carbon was one of the TV series that got me through 2020. So while I loved watching both seasons at the time, I also remembered very little about them when I saw the audio books on sale in 2025. Everything came flooding back as soon as I started listening to the first book though, which I quickly realised had been followed almost scene-for-scene by the first season of the TV series. Where things got very interesting though was listening to books 2 and 3 (Broken Angels and Woken Furies). I’d read a lot of complaints online about the 2nd season of the Netflix series, and watching it in 2020 I hadn’t really understood what the problem was… But reading the trilogy and then rewatching the 2nd season made it abundantly clear that Netflix had carved up both books and botched them both over 8 episodes. Broken Angels shifts completely away from the first book’s police procedural approach and into an incredible war story - putting Takeshi Kovacs in his absolute element, while developing more of the alien “Elder” mythology. Woken Furies takes that even further by recovering Quillcrest Falconer and putting an Elder in the same mind, and setting the whole thing on Takeshi’s home planet of Harlans World. These books are extraordinary (while also being pretty gratuitous with both sex and violence) but it’s pretty clear Netflix tried to take the best of both without allowing the space to develop characters or plot properly. Having the Netflix series end with the door left open for another season felt disingenuous too - these books are great reads and we’ll worth your time, so the biggest gripe is that the 2nd season of the TV series didn’t do either of them any justice.
The Combat Doctor - Dan Pronk This is one of those books that Audbile recommended to me for a low time before I finally decided to use a credit to see what the fuss was about… And I’m glad I did. Dr Dan Pronk served with Australian special forces in Afghanistan around the same time I was training with the British Royal Marines, and much of what he describes reflects what I was seeing of life
Cryptonomicon - Neal Stephenson
Bhagavad Gita - Anonymous This is one of those religious texts that I’d always been interested in reading for general understanding, but also wanted an objective interpretation of the text and didn’t really know where to start in finding one. In the end it was as easy as seeing a highly rated audio book version and buying it. This is a relatively short book (a long poem if we’re being exact) and I listened to all of it in a single sitting, and the translator’s introduction and recap at the end really helped set the initial context and to clarify the important details. I have a kindle copy of this too, but I’m not sure I’ll ever read it - the audibook version was perfect, and allowed me to dip in and out of parts I might not have followed or pushed through but which got the perfect explanation at the end in the recap.
Wayne Dyer’s Ultimate Library - Wayne Dyer This is a behemoth of an audio book, and it pulls snippets from Wayer Dyer’s lectures across more than 30 years. An old friend I’ve lost touch with (and who I sadly suspect might have passed away) used to love listening to Wayne Dyer lectures, and so listening to this allowed me to reconnect to them in a way. There’s no doubt that Wayne Dyer represented a beautiful and clear view on spirituality and the way we interact with each other and the universe, and this was quickly added to my Audible favourites so it’s ready for a future relisten.
Starship Troopers - Robert Heinlein My first exposure to Starship Troopers was the 1997 film, which could not be more different from the book itself, but both of them continue to be fascinating pieces of literature. I first read the Starhip Troopers novel by Robert Heinlein when I was bumping in and out of hostels in London after passing the PRMC to join the Royal Marines in mid 2009, but prior to starting training with them towards the end of 2009. Revisiting it 16 years later, it’s all the more obvious that Heinlein’s perspective on war is much more complex than many commentators gave him credit for. The Verhoven film remains a masterclass in satire, but the novel feels like someone who had experienced war trying to come to grips with both it’s abject horror and the elation of being part of a larger mission (and how easily that can be hijacked and twisted into fascism). This is still a remarkable read (and relatively short) but it certainly didn’t have the impact this time that it did when I read it before starting training with the RM - I’m a different person doing different things with a radically different perspective on warfare after leaving the military behind a decade and a half ago.
Agent to the Stars - John Scalzi John Scalzi has quickly become a regular sci-fi favourite of mine ever since I read “The Kaji Appreciation Society” a few years ago. This kept being recommended in Audible, and I was looking for something to break up the mammoth Wayne Dyer I’d just finished. If anything this was more about the way Hollywood works than it was about aliens, but like so much of John Scalzi’s novels this was all about taking a central sci-fi idea and letting the different characters interact and play around it. Some of the plot points towards the end felt very obvious, but that didn’t stop it from being a really engaging and funny read - if there’s one thing I love about John Scalzi books is that even the serious ones are packed with humour, and this one was particularly funny from start to finish.
I’m Glad My Mom Died - Jennette McCurdy I went into this book with absolutely no idea who Jeanette McCurdy was or why she’d written a book about how she was glad her mother was dead - I picked it up purely because it’d been recommended by Audible and I figured she was a comedian who’d written a satirical book with her Mom’s death as a dark punchline. What I really didn’t expect was to read a book by a world-famous child actor who was bared her soul to share the way how she had been physically, emotionally, and sexually abused by her deeply troubled mother in pursuit of stardom in Hollywood. This book completely sideswiped me, and for the longest time I considered trying to contact Jeanette to thank her for writing something so unbelievably raw and funny. I’m certain if I had written to her it would have been lost in the torrent of messages I’m sure she receives from her iCarly fans, but I genuinely knew nothing about iCarly going into this book - I’m just in awe that someone could write something so honest that was simultaneously horrifying and hilarious. I never thought I’d say this about a memoir from someone most known for a Disney kids show I knew nothing about, but reading “I’m Glad My Mom Died” simultaneously made me want to be a better writer and to email an author I’d never heard of before to simply say thank you. So Jeanette if you ever read this - thank you, and please never stop writing.
Redshirts - John Scalzi This is easily the best example I’ve read of John Scalzi’s style as he takes a sci-fi idea and stretches it as far as he can. There are a couple of interesting plotting elements that were added early on that took most of the book to fully come to grips with, UT for the most part this was a very fun and meta reading experience. I broke this audiobook up with “Fahrenheit-182” by Mark Hoppus as I was driving out to the Nullarbor on a cave diving expedition, switching between them one chapter at a time, and it was always tempting to sneak an extra chapter of Redshirts whenever John Scalzi left the chapter on a cliffhanger.
Farenheit-182 - Mark Hoppus My exposure to Blink-182 started with a friend’s copy of “Dude Ranch”, and I’ll even admit to hunting down a copy of “Cheshire Cat” in my final year of high school, but like many people I became a real fan when “Enema of the State” was released. It’s the only album that I’ve ever had my Mum suggest I keep somewhere else - not because of the lyrics, but because the front cover is a stripper in a busty nurse costume who’s seductively/threatengly pulling on a rubber glove, and 15 year old Josh genuinely didn’t realise it might be a problem. All of that to say that Mark Hoppus’s memoir gave me a far greater appreciation for who Blink-182 is and why they’ve one through the various evolutions they have over the last 25 years I’ve listened to their music. The sheer grind of there early touring was inspiring, and something that I guess many rock & punk bands have to do in the early days, but the utter punishment of 3 dudes living in a van, driving through the night to get to the next venue, and counting penny’s to buy a McDonald’s breakfast each morning, all so they could play for 20 minutes in some dive bar - that level of commitment is both inspiring and crazy, and it reminded me of the desperate determination I saw in comics trying to break through in the UK and the lengths they’d go to because they believed deep down they simply HAD to perform. I also didn’t realise that Mark Hoppus had undergone an absolutely brutal chemotherapy treatment in 2020, and it’s nice to know that after all the ugly shit that had happened within the band through the years that Tom Delonge was the first person on the phone when the news of Mark’s treatments broke. This was a generally wonderful read, although I’ll admit that relistening to the albums as I was reading the book wasn’t as fun as I’d hoped - it’s pretty clear my interest in Blink-182’s music hasn’t moved much since I was in high school, so while it was awesome to hear Dude Ranch and Enema of the State again, and parts of California too, there was zero nostalgia for Self-Titled, Neighbourhoods, Eight, or the recent albums when Tom returned.
Wanderlust - Reid Mitenbuler I’d been inadvertently paying for audiobook access through Spotify for awhile, so when I realised I cancelled the subscription but still wanted to make the most of the remaining month while I had it - “Wanderlust” popped up as a recommendation and I’m really glad it did. This audiobook was what I listened to each morning as I started each day of my expedition to the Nullarbor, and there was a strange juxtaposition of listening to the biography of one of the main characters in the Heroic Age of Arctic exploration while cooking breakfast before climbing down a hole in the desert to discover and map new underwater passages. Knowing there’s a painting of Peter Fryken in the Explorer’s Club in NYC makes me want to visit all the more to appreciate this unique and big-hearted character who discovered more of the world while making it better by being in it - I wish I’d had the chance to meet him, but this book is the next best thing.
Eon - Greg Bear This book was an absolute trip for so many different reasons, the biggest because I kept being confused about when it had been written. While it’s at it’s heart a pretty mind-bending sci-fi story about an artificial space created by future humans which accidentally loops back to a critical time in Earth’s history, the heart of the story is set in the 2020’s (eg. Now) and the yet it delves into all sorts of mindsets and geopolitics that feel more at home in the 1970’s and 80’s (specifically the US’s relations with the Soviet Union and China). The audiobook was also published in 2020 which makes reading it in 2025 feel like it was intended as an alternate history novel. It was only when I realised the original book had been written in the 1980s that I realised that it had been written as genuine sci-fi and not alternate history, and Greg Bear wasn’t trying to do some some of interesting “What If this happened instead” story from the context of the 2020’s but a “What if this happens in the future” based in the politics and attitudes of the 1980s. I won’t say it’s particularly well-written, but as a concept the book is pretty incredible and highlights the cyclic nature of time and reality that I think we’re still struggling with as a species.
Down with the System - Serj Tankian System of a Down has always been one of those bans that I grew up obsessing over at different times in my life but then just as quickly forgot about. I’d always been interested in Serj Tankian’s story though, so when I saw he’d written a memoir I figured it was time to understand more about the guy who I’d always assumed was a pretty typical rocker who’d been the primary creative force behind SOAD and had used the platform to discuss the Armenian genocide. What I hadn’t realised was that Derren had always been the musical heart of the band, and that Serj was really the vocal artist who’d been adding the flourishes and quirks to what Derren was really directing. I also didn’t realise that the band hadn’t put out an album in nearly two decades, or that there had been so much in-fighting. Reading Serj’s memoir, it also seems like he didn’t realise he’d pissed the others so much. True to Serj’s style though, he’s respectfully honest and vulnerable about the band’s challenges and holds absolutely no bitterness towards his band brothers, even when the Trump-supporting politics of John (SOAD’s drummer and Serj’s brother-in-law) are so existentially-opposed to Serj’s own left leaning tendencies.

content:
I’ve just started my journey to Antarctica, or more accurately I’ve started the first overseas step to Antarctica with the flight from Melbourne to Santiago, and I’m getting used to working on the small Bluetooth keyboard I bought to avoid my laptop. This trip will be the first major test of this, not only learning to use a small form keyboard like this, but also the experience of travelling without a laptop - something I haven’t done since I left the marines.
Already I’m seeing the benefit of shifting to somesting smaller and electronic. -There is simply no way I’d be typing on my laptop right now, as I’d be concerned about power usage, turbulence, and that lunch is likely to be served in the near future so I’d need to find somewhere to tuck the laptop during that. Likewise, there is absolutely no way I could be writing in a journal right now, as the turbulence we currently have would easily put me off as I tried to scrawl on the page.
I won’t pretend that this small form keyboard isn’t a challenge, although I seem to be getting a bit of a feel for it and I appreciate that my spellchecker is correcting the obvious typos I’m still making as I adjust. The biggest hesitation I’m currently experiencing while typing is the apostrophe as I try to type things like “aren’t” and “I’m” while being forced to use the function key instead of simply shift. I get that it’s a space-saving element that allows the L & ; keys to do double service with ’ & " alts respectively, but it’ s still awkward and a clear disruption to the flow that I can feel myself getting into when I don’t need to use an apostrophe (stumbling over “don’t” just then is another example).
The apostrophe issue aside though, I particularly love that I haven’t needed to bring a large device with me for this trip - everything I need can be handled by my phone. This keyboard has felt like a waste previously given I also like to journal, and the only time I’d like to go somewhere without a laptop is a local Cafe or travelling, but it’s exciting to consider that I’ll be doing this trip from a small mobile device instead. I’m going to Antarctica, and I don’t need a laptop, or a full size camera, or very much at all. If I weren’t diving in Ushuaia then I likely would have left the GoPro behind too, although I suspect that will do plenty of work while kayaking too.
My laptop does a wonderful job, and I have no doubt it’ll be vital for work and other trips in the future. But for a journey such as this where I don’t need to review data or anything else that requires screen real estate, then this folding keyboard is going to be perfect and it’ll encourage me to write when I otherwise might now. And anything that supports me writing more than I have in the past is something to be valued and endorsed.

content:
As I put together the final things ready for the next few weeks in Antarctica and then Perth, I’m asking myself what my outstanding obligations are. This can be my emotional obligations (like people and things I feel I owe something to), physical obligations (like things that I have and feel responsible for), and my own spiritual obligations (the things that I feel I need to work on or do to feel fulfilled).
Looking at my physical obligations is probably the easiest place to start, as they’re tangible and obvious. I have a wide range of different things that I currently own which I feel require attention, as well as things which I likely haven’t given enough thought to. My diving gear is the most obvious “obligation” which I see, and it concerns me that I decent chunk of that is hidden away in the storage unit. Things like the compressor and it’s spare parts certainly bugs me, and it’s certainly a breach of that idea that if you can’t carry it then you can’t keep it. I’ll be keen to sell that compressor when I get back, as well as anything else which I have that doesn’t have an immediate purpose.
I’m generally pretty good about getting rid of excess physical things, but the few things which I do hang onto and don’t use generally have an emotional obligation attached to them too. My bookcase is a classic example of that - full of unread books that I’d “love” to read and yet haven’t made a priority to actually open. Part of that has been my effort to read the 101 Things books first, and yet that hasn’t been a priority either. I’d very much like to read those books while I’m away, and there’s every reason to believe that’s possible - make it a priority when you’re not writing.
The other physical/emotional obligation I have is my ukulele, which has sat unloved by your office door for years. I know that right now I have a backlog on artistic expression, and I’m tackling that through writing (specifically by writing these Mini Essays) but my ukulele is important, and just like writing it’s an artistic expression which is vital to my mental, emotional and spiritual wellbeing. Just like writing, it needs to be made more of a priority in the year ahead - it needs to be something that is important to you, and if you’re embarrassed by how others might react then simply close the office door.
Spiritual obligations are really the ones I’ve most ignored over the last few years, and the ones that I most need to reconnect with to express and free myself from the mindset I’m trying to escape from. I have an obligation to pay attention to synchronicity when it occurs, an obligation to celebrate joy and to embrace the ebb and flow of the universe. I haven’t paid attention to the subtle notes of life for awhile, and I have a real concern that if I continue to ignore it then I’ll lose the ability to hear those messages that have made some many parts of my life feel special in the past.
The truth is I don’t have many “obligations”, but the ones I have are very important, and it’s vital I meet them more regularly than I have over the last few years. I have an obligation to the physical things I’m responsible for, to my mental and emotional wellbeing, and an obligation to my spiritual practice that has been severely undernourished. Make a solid effort to convert the “obligations” you have into remarkable things - read books and publish notes on them, develop ideas and publish books on them, look after your dive gear and discover new caves with it, and pay attention to the universe around you so you can more fully appreciate all it’s intricacies.

content:
What do you really want to do before you die? It’s a tough question, and one that’s even tougher to contemplate. You’re 40 in a few months, which is wild considering you never thought you’d make it to 30. Now you talk about being lucky to make 70… maybe you need to ask yourself why you didn’t think you’d make it to 30, as well as what you’d do if you made it to 80 and have another 40 years of life ahead of you.
But the question is what you want to do before you die, and not if you’ll live to 80. You want to shed all the excess, all the attachments you have - to be a completed book without loose ends or appendices. You have books to write, and it’s nice to acknowledge that you’d spend your last days writing if you could. It’s not about being remembered, it’s about creating something you put your whole soul into, something that utterly consumes you, that pours out of you like water, that merges with you as a person where the book is as much you as you are it.
Setting an arbitrary number of books to write before you die is meaningless, especially if you just use it as a timeline to measure and wipe yourself with. Writing articles for magazines and journals means less too - it’s like you’re doing 5-10 minute comedy sets again. It doesn’t mean you can’t or won’t, but the real fulfilment comes from writing full length books that you are truly proud of in the end.
You have so many adventures behind you that feel like emotional boat anchors, dragging along the ocean floor and tripping you up as you look at them and think “coulda, woulda, shoulda”. Well you have absolutely nothing to lose - write. Don’t worry about if you’re writing the right thing or not, just develop the things that you know are calling to you now. Don’t be afraid to start, fuck up, change course, and start again - none of this is wasted, and returning every day to write a mini essay is exactly the kind of writing muscle you need to develop so you can write thousands of words a day again as you focus on a book.
So don’t worry about trying to tick things off a bucket list before you die for the sake of it - figure out what you’re going to do today, how to use the winds of circumstance to push you towards who you want to be every day, and then get up tomorrow to be a little bit better at being that person tomorrow. This is the way of the peaceful warrior, and you’ll never “achieve” it - you can only walk it each day.

title: Mini Essay - What do you really want to do before you die

content:
This morning you spent a lot of time thinking during your walk about what fear means to you. There were a lot of examples, but actually pinning it down felt really hard, and much of that comes down to it being similar to distinctively different to anxiety.
For me, fear is cold followed by force. Fear is something you tend to run at, something you feel and immediately react to with action. Fear isn’t the every day concerns of things not working out or of something hypothetically happening - that’s anxiety. Fear is trying to hold a door closed as three sailors smash into it from the other side to kill you and rape the two women in the room with you. Fear is grabbing the fire extinguisher off the wall and breaking the toes in the foot jammed in the same door. Fear is holding onto a plastic sheet carrying a friend as they’re dying of hypothermia, as you run through the mud to get him into the back of an ambulance, then someone to help peel your fingers from the plastic because your hand has cramped onto it. Fear is going back to camp afterwards and finding two more, and knowing there’s no one left to help but you. Fear is talking your Mum through all the things she needs to put in a Go-Bag, because you’re sure that your father is going to try and kill her. Fear is begging her not to wait until he breaks in one night, to leave and get out now. Fear is him finding out where she’s been hiding, and having him threaten to fly across the country to kill her as well as my sister and her family too. Fear is knowing exactly what you’d to him do if he ever did.
I’m not sure Dune got it quite right with “Fear is the mind killer” - I think anxiety is the real mind killer. Fear sharpens everything to down a point, and it’s at that point that you find out if you fight, flee, or freeze. It’s a point that gives you a decision to act or not act. Fear isn’t about being overwhelmed either - that’s panic, and you’ve known that too. Fear is a very distinct experience, where you know exactly what you need to do to survive (or keep someone else alive) and you just need to do it.
So for you, anxiety is that lurking concern that erodes your wellbeing - it’s a poison that seeps in and makes you overthink all the “what ifs” of your situation. Anxiety is worrying about falling off a rope when you’re already on it. Panic is a loss of control, where your monkey brain takes over and screams a single overwhelming thought like “GET OUT!” or “BREATHE!”. But fear is something else altogether - it’s clear, cold, and unforgiving. Fear says “Do this, or you’ll die”. And you simply do it… or you die.
References Mini Essay - Fear Is The Mind Killer
title: Mini Essay - What is fear to you

content:
There’s no denying that the last few months have been pretty turbulent, and I have a whole series of fairly significant life changes heading my way in the next month too. My perspective on life has massively shifted since turning 40 in August, leaving ElectraNet in September, and especially since Trip - Antarctica - 2025 Nov so it’s natural to look ahead and wonder where I’m trying to go next.
While everyone seems to put a lot of focus on turning 40, having drinks with Cairo last night reminded me that I’m still a massive Htchhikers Guide to the Galaxy nerd so I’ve always been more curious about what my life would look like at age 42. I’ll hit that milestone in August 2027, so I’m really curious about what my life is going to look like 4 months after that in 2028.
Between now and then I’ll be finally embracing my desire to live in the VW Transporter; I’ll have the experience and certifications to do any kind of Cyber Security work I want (realistically I’m already at that point, but even more so with my plans for 2026), and I’ll have achieved a lifelong dream of diving at Bikini Atoll as part of Trip - Bikini Atoll - 2028 June. So the real question is what I’d like to do after all of that? And what do I want to do to prepare for the life I want to live at age 42?
Working in Antarctica is the most obvious option right now. After the experience of Trip - Antarctica - 2025 Nov I know that I absolutely the incrediblely stark and beautiful nature of the place, but I also know I don’t want to go back as a tourist or really as a tour guide. I’d love to do that in the Arctic, but there’s a huge part of me that desperately wants to truly live and work in that environment for an extended period of time. I’m keenly aware that it’d disconnect me from #diving for an extended period, but it’d also disconnect me from much of my current life too, and that has a lot of appeal. It’s not that I want to disappear from the world, but I’d like to turn the noise down and be pulled in fewer directions at once. In the same way I love organising a pet/housesit so I can work on a book, I love the idea of extended disconnection from the outside world so I can work on the things that I truly care about.
The idea of studying for a masters in Slovenia is also present, but the more I reflect on it the more I realise that I’ve been down this path before - my physical degree is still at a university in the Netherlands because I was deadset about enrolling in a masters there, then realised that a return to uni would be interesting but wouldn’t actually move me forward very much. Anything that I find interesting, I could (and likely should) write a book about instead. There are so many books I’d like to write, and the ideas clog up the longer they go untapped, so studying for something that doesn’t have a clear outcome (like studying for a CISA certification as a pathway to becoming an IRAP Assessor) doesn’ make a whole lot of sense, but I know I get wrapped up in the enthusiasm of how cool it’d be to live in another country and study something I’m passionate about. Do you need to do that within a university framework? No, but that doesn’t mean you need to reject the idea outright - just be very wary of allowing the fantasy override the practicalities of investing in the idea.
The are many other things on your Bucket List and 101 Things - To Do which I want to put energy into, but they don’t leap to mind right now without looking at them. One thing that I might also look at doing is a Long Solo - getting on a bike, kayak, or even on foot to cover a significant distance. Much like the idea of Study - Masters though, there kind of needs to be a reason to get to the end of it. Is it about Writing Books? There are far too many other things you want to write about more than what it’s like being on the move for months. The one thing that you know you can do endlessly is write, so having the achievement of a Long Solo would be nice, there are plenty of other things in my past to be proud of already, and I’d rather write about them first.
So what do I want to be doing in 2028 after turning 42? I want to be a travelling author. I might be in Antarctica, I might be on a boat travelling the world, I might be living in a wood cabin by a lake in a pine forest… But whatever it is I’m doing, I want to be working on writing Books. Everything else is a way of experiencing the world so I can create stories in my Writing. So keep doing the things you’re doing and working towards what you’ve made a priority, but remember that in two years you want to be doing things that directly support writing more books, rather than hindering or distracting me from the goal of writing 10 books in your life.

content:
As you sit in the airport at Buenos Aires after such a hefty few days of flying, it’s starting to really dawn on me that I’m about to flying to Ushuaia - the gateway to Antarctica. And in just a few days, I’ll be getting onboard an expedition ship Going to the Antarctic Peninsula!
There’s a big part of me that is simply not processing that fact - that in a few days I’ll be in Antarctica. I’m not sure if it’s the numbness you’ve experienced a lot of these last few years, but it’s not clear if my lack of excitement is because I haven’t come to terms with the reality of the trip yet, or if I’m downplaying it all in an attempt to protect my psyche from potential disappointment.
What is clear is that I’m not overly excited, and I wonder if that’s just always been my way? Thinking back I’ve often done the same thing before big trips - busy getting things ready, other bullshit things popping up that demand attention, and just general tiredness from juggling too many priorities at once. Likely a combination of all these things which are slowing you down from unbridled enthusiasm. But I think this trip will cut through much of that - you’re off on a lifelong dream to see the white continent, and you’re doing all you can to see leopard seals while kayaking. That is going to be fucking WILD.
Even as you type that though, you’re trying to downplay it and be fine with it not happening. It was genuinely tough to write :That is going to be fucking WILD" because there’s part of you that is adding doubt to protect yourself from it not happening. But you don’t need protecting - you need to throw yourself out there and be wrong instead! Say “I’m going to Antarctica to kayak with leopard seals because it’s something I’ve always dreamed of.” and don’t try to protect your ego by adding caveats. Do you have control over what the leopard seals do? No! Will you be disappointed if you don’t see any? Probably! But will it ruin the entire trip? FUCK NO! Because this is all about putting yourself out there, making bold claims, and then owning it when things don’t work out as hoped or planned.
You had someone at your last job who could never commit to any thing or any measurable statement - it was always qualified with a whole lot of bullshit and hand-waving so he couldn’t be pinned to any specific statement later. I fear that my lack of enthusiasm for life might be stemming from a cynicism and insecurity about the things I do - that I’ve spent too long taking people’s comments personally that I’ve been Self-censoring and adding caveats to everything. YOU DO NOT NEED TO BE RIGHT ABOUT ANYTHING! Be wrong! Be wrong on a regular basis, and be okay with it, because being wrong makes life more interesting - it makes for a better story, and it makes you stronger too!
So why is Antarctica so important to you? Because this trip is an opportunity to be raw and open and honest about how much this shit excites you! Fuck, you’re about to fly to the southern-most tip of South America (a continent you’ve never been to before!) and then get on a fucking boat to the bottom of the world! You’re going to rock and roll through the Drake Passage, you’re going to see an absolute shitton of penguins and seals, and you’re going to see leopard seals fucking them all up!
This is an important, expensive, and exciting trip - stop trying to protect yourself from disappointment and start living life as fully as you can as you experience things you love!

content:
Writing a book about cave diving isn’t just the “right thing to do”, it’s also something I genuinely love the idea of doing. Writing is a huge part of my life and how I process things over time, and Diving is equally important to me having been part of my life for nearly 30 of my 40 years now. Cave diving is something that I’m fiercely passionate about and incredibly invested in, so it makes sense that I’d be drawn to the idea of combining these interests into writing a book about cave diving, especially if I put it in the context of my first 500 cave dives.
Beyond the most obvious elements though, I know that writing a book about cave diving is important to both the sport and myself. I’m a good and engaging writer, and I know deep down that writing is where I excel - the artform that I know I’m strongest at, where I can make the greatest impact. Likewise, I am an exceptional cave diver with a natural instinct for finding new tunnel where others couldn’t. Discovering and sharing new tunnel with people, being able to show non-divers why we do the dives we do, and embracing that raw sense of exploration all help me be a better version of myself.
There’s also no doubt that a lot has happened in the last 6 years too, as much above water as below. Right now I have a lot of strong feelings about the Australian cave diving community and the way I’ve been treated by specific parts of it over the last couple of years. There’s no question I’m angry and hurt about some of it, but that’s not my motivation for writing this book - if it were, I’d have thrown the idea out months ago. But I know this is a worthwhile project to pursue, specifically because I’m worried that my anger over the vindictive and petty politics will spill out into a book that might encourage others to engage with cave diving. I genuinely love this sport, and the last thing I’d want would be to write something that put people off it because of the old-boy politics that goes on.
I have numerous things that I could write, and probably plenty of other things that in some ways I should write before a book on cave diving… but I know this is the right thing to do. If I were to switch my daily Mini Essays over to writing about various dives I’ve done, I have no doubt I’d be able to create this book in a matter of months. Better yet, I’d love to turn my daily Mini Essays into a project to write up the 101 Things that I’ve completed, and then allocate a separate hour each day to writing about my 500 cave dives.
Part of me worries that I’ll need more time to write these things than I’m currently willing to give, or that I won’t write them properly because I’m trying to make them fit into the #mini-essay format. But those are both poor excuses for procrastination - ultimately this is just about showing up and writing the next thing on the list. The Book - 101 Things will be incredibly straight forward because you just need to write the next entry on the 101 Things - Complete List list. Likewise with your cave diving book, you just need to write about the next dive. That may mean putting together a list of your cave diving experiences so you can simply pick the next entry and start writing about it, but creating that list should be fairly straight-forward (especially if you add “Make a list of cave dives” to your Tasks).
So why am I writing a book about cave diving? Because I have some incredible experiences to share and stories to tell - I saw that first hand talking to Mitch and Keith at the bottom of Murra El Elevyn when I was causally dropping stories while sorting out gear that was blowing the minds of them both. I’m writing this book because people are interested in what I do, the cave diving stories are particularly great, and I love sharing experiences with people who are interested.
As I write this book, just remember that “interesting” is the key. My goal with Cosmic Nomad was to make it as funny as possible, but that’s not the aim this time around. In the wise words of Ivor Dembina, “You don’t always have to be funny, but you do have to be interesting.”

content:
Related:
One of the challenges I routinely face is trying to prioritise writing as a regular practice. or as any kind of practice, regular or not. I know that I love writing, and even as I type this I can feel that sense of creation that I truly crave whenever I sit down and start typing out my thoughts on a keyboard - a particularly visceral experience where each click of the keyboard is another step towards an artistic expression that’s yearning to be shared.
Over and over again however, I find myself either distracted or making other things a priority over sitting down to write something I really want to write. There is SO much in my Mini Essays document which is just begging to be written about, and that’s not even taking into account all the writing I want to do towards a cave diving book, all the writing I’d like to do about the cave diving sites I love, or all the writing you have queued up around the #101-Things and your #bucket-list.
There is an extraordinary amount of writing that you genuinely want to do, but time and time again you find yourself trying to finish other tasks before you’ll write. Today is a classic example - you made writing a mini essay your highest priority for today, and you’re only just sitting here typing it out at 9pm after a full day of doing other shit. Was that other shit important? Absolutely! You spent a significant chunk of today fixing your Digital Garden so that you can better share the notes and ideas that you have. But was it the highest priority for today? Certainly not.
I think part of the challenge is not feeling inspired to write about certain things when you sit down. But you also know that inspiration is bullshit - you simply need to write, and the inspiration comes from turning your creative outlet into a habit and an obsession. You have an extraordinarily long list of potential mini essay topics to write about already, so there’s no reason why you can’t glance at any one of them and start typing. In fact, the entire point of the mini-essays is to start writing when you’re NOT inspired! They’re there to lower the barrier to entry on writing - something that doesn’t mean much, but you can use to process ideas in a quick and easy way without being too invested on whether the writing is good or not. Assume the writing is bad, but simply get writing and turn it into a habit.
The idea of making writing a priority/habit/obsession is all about turning up to work on it every day. My journal is good for processing things on a personal level, and it’s nice to slow down and write things out by hand. But what I write there is never going to be published (burning my journals still feels important) and something certainly changes when you know that your writing may have an audience (however small). Journaling the things that shouldn’t be said aloud seems vital to my mental health, but not as important as writing out my ideas and making them available for others to read too.
So how do I make writing a priority and avoid being distracted? Easy - you make writing something that you must do each day. Journaling doesn’t count: you need to make sure that you write something each day that could be read by other humans. It may have taken you until 9pm tonight to sit down and write this, but you’ve done it, and 20 mins later you’re struggling to wrap this up into a conclusion because you want to keep typing.
Make writing for publication a priority for each day, even if it’s just a mini essay (most of them will probably be mini essays), and before you go to bed each night you need to set a plan on what to write the next day. You can even build it into your Template - Mini Essay - add “tomorrow’s mini essay” to the template so that you can put down some sort of plan for the next day before you close out today.

content:
Throughout most of my 20’s I was certain I wouldn’t be alive to turn 30. It’s not like I can pinpoint exactly where that idea came from, but there’s no question it was a recurring belief that shaped the way I thought and planned my life. If I try to trace it back, I suspect I’ll wind up back at April 19th, 2008. I made a choice that night to live, and it was certainly a close-call, but I’ve used that night as a reference for most of my life since - no matter what awful shit I’ve been through since then, I know that I will never allow myself to be trapped in that mindset ever again, where suicide felt like the only way out.
But I know those thoughts didn’t suddenly disappear that night just because I made a decision to live. Looking back on it more than 17 years later, I think that sense of despair evolved from feeling helplessly trapped and suicidal, and it became a sense that I’d die in the next few years doing something ridiculous. Not because I actually wanted to die, or that I was seeking out an end, but simply because I was throwing my full force at things and activities that made death by misadventure likely.
Breaking out of that depressive-suicidal cycle, I think I started thinking “I got through my darkest valley, so now it doesn’t matter what happens”. In many ways that’s exactly that healthy mindset I needed and still want to cultivate. Where it went too far was signing up for dangerous, awful things because I didn’t think staying alive mattered at all. I remember thinking that the French Foreign Legion or the British Royal Marines were the only places I might feel a sense of belonging, because shooting and blowing things up were “all I was good for”. Because I was still hurting, and I thought at least I could die through circumstances I created rather than directly ending it myself. I didn’t think I’d make it to 30 because I believed I’d die in a firefight or trying to defuse an IED - not because I wanted to serve the greater good, but because that’s all I thought I was good for, and maybe I’d die doing something that might matter.
Seeing what I saw in the marines, it was pretty clear that shit regularly happens to good people and it doesn’t mean anything in the grand scheme of things. Realising that is why I left - because awful, meaningless things would happen to people I cared about, and I didn’t want to be the person I needed to be to survive and protect others in an environment where people often died through meaningless violence.
Leaving the military didn’t fix the sense that I had nothing to offer though, and if I’m honest it made it even worse. I didn’t slip back into seeking death through suicide - I’d never allow myself to be mentally trapped in that space again. But I did still see death before 30 as an “inevitable relief”, and I think that only started to change with Mars One.
Suddenly Mars One gave me the opportunity for a “death” that would be worthwhile and 10 years away - after that “inevitable” end point of 30. I had a reason to get out of bed every day, because I was working towards something extraordinary. Something that would help people, which gave me a sense of meaning, and would still provide the sense of finality that I seemed to need. Leaving for Mars would be a relief, because I could let go of the complications and pain of life on Earth, and serve humanity by being as far away from it as possible.
Losing Mars One hurt me profoundly, and it continues to taunt me as that thing I put every once of my being into for 10 years which eventually just dissolved. Mars One gave me a reason to look forward to a life beyond 30, and now that I’m 40 I wonder what meaning I get from the life I live today? In some ways my life doesn’t matter at all - I’m just one human of billions that’s wandering around this planet doing things and trying to find meaning from it. But I’m still here, and I still have the opportunity to live, breathe, and help others every day.
There are so many things that I would never have experienced or learned about myself if I’d made a different choice on that night in April 2008 - rediscovering my passion for science and exploration through Mars One for starters. And there are so many extraordinary things I’ve been lucky enough to do in the last 10 years since I turned 30 - I’ve written two books, toured globally as a comedian, met astronauts, discovered caves, owned a cave diving hostel, and been celebrated as a world-class explorer. In less than two weeks I’ll be on my next extraordinary adventure in Antarctica!
I’m incredibly lucky to be here, and I can’t even begin to imagine what kind of incredible experiences I’ll have over the next 10 years if I’m still alive at 50. I don’t want to die, but I’m going to make damn sure that when I do go I’ll do it with my stories told and no doubt in anyone’s mind that I made the most of the time I had.

content:
Now that you’ve been suspended by the CDAA, you have an amazing opportunity to look ahead and ask what kind of future you want to have in cave diving. You knew the suspension was coming, and you’ve been more than emotionally ready to tackle it - part of you has even relished it finally coming to pass. So the question now is how you want to develop as an exploration cave diver outside of Mt Gambier and the CDAA.
First and foremost you’re heading to Sulawesi to dive and chat to Robin Cuesta, which presents exciting opportunities for both your podcast and to discuss the importance of water security. A major point of interest for your cave exploration is to give it a purpose and scientific legitimacy - you want to explore not just for the sake of exploring, but to also bring back valuable data and to help the people who are responsible for the land you’re diving under.
Your future also involves diving outside of Mt Gambier, and mostly outside of Australia for that matter too. There’s no doubt you want to visit incredible places and to help others see them too - your real interest is in making adventures easier for everyone so they can support the exploration too. At the heart of this however is your own desire to explore, experience and share cave diving with others - to tap into that passion for an “underground Google Maps” that you dreamed of so many years ago. That means having a list of places you want to explore AND to collect publishable data from. It’s not enough to just see these places and take a select few - you really want to share these places with anyone who’s interested, to feed that passion for adventure, and to do good science so we can understand these places better.
So ask yourself - where do you want to cave dive, and how can you collect great data to support the production of incredible maps and models for the places you visit? Even the most touristy caves don’t have 3D models, so don’t just go for the most difficult or remote places you can think of - dives like Mjonar Janos and Gozo are absolutely worth the journey. And don’t worry about how you’ll fit this around work - you have the resources to do these things, so plan them out and make them happen. Whatever you figure out with work, you’ll be able to support yourself and see the places you want to see.
First priority? Figure out how to get Lewy to the Eastern Mediterranean, and make sure you record that journey. Taking Australia’s pre-eminent underwater cave geologist on his dream trip would be an extraordinary thing to do, and there’s only so many years available to do it.

content:
Ask yourself “What is your evil secret plan?”. Ultimately this is a question about how you’re going to use the system to do the things that YOU want to do and live the life you want to live. We’re not talking about blindly trying to “Live your dreams” - we’re talking about gaming the system so it looks like you’re playing along with everyone else, but you’re hacking the game so you do exactly what you want regardless of what others may expect or even demand of you. So you’re not playing by any rules, but you are faking compliance while you put all the pieces into place to subvert expectations.
For you, it’s clear you want to explore the universe and share those experiences with others through videos and books - it’s where your interest in Jacques Cousteau comes from. Under the current paradigm you need an income to live, to travel, and to share the adventures you go on - I’m not interested in trying to subvert Capitalism, but it doesn’t mean I’m not a Communist at heart. So you need to earn money, but that’s just a tool for doing what you really want to do.
My evil secret plan is to subvert the muggle world and live like a folk legend. You want folks to say “Yeah, I met Josh Richards - he was doing some ridiculous shit and then he disappeared again”.
My evil secret plan is to never let the muggles know what I’ll do next - to have layers they’ll never touch, to have connections and stories from every corner of human experience, and to leave the people I meet wondering how the fuck I’ve done all this shit in the time I’ve had, knowing they’ll never understand.
My evil secret plan is earn enough money to turn up in all sorts of weird places whenever it suits, to carry out random acts of kindness, and to disappear again. I don’t want stability or infrastructure or predictability - I want to adapt to unexpected chaos and to keep moving forward as the universe throws new and unusual things at me.
My evil secret plan is that there is no plan - I’m just tacking my way through the flow of the universe. If I feel the wind changing, then I’ll work with it. If the drops to nothing, I’ll wait. But when it picks up again, I’ll use it - to go with it, to tack into it, or to cut across it. It doesn’t matter - what does matter is that you explore the universe and you share it with others who won’t go to the places or situations that you will.

content:
Usually, when something gets warmed up, heat tends to spread outward before eventually dissipating. But things are a little different in the world of superfluid quantum gas. For the first time, MIT scientists have successfully imaged how heat actually travels in a wave, known as a “second sound,” through this exotic fluid. Understanding this dynamic could help answer questions about high-temperature superconductors and neutron stars. In the world of average, everyday materials, heat tends to spread out from a localized source. Drop a burning coal into a pot of water, and that liquid will slowly rise in temperature before its heat eventually dissipates. But the world is full of rare, exotic materials that don’t exactly play by these thermal rules.
Instead of spreading out as one would expect, these superfluid quantum gasses “slosh” heat side to side—it essentially propagates as a wave. Scientists call this behavior a material’s “second sound” (the first being ordinary sound via a density wave). Although this phenomenon has been observed before, it’s never been imaged. But recently, scientists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) were finally able to capture this movement of pure heat by developing a new method of thermography (a.k.a. heat-mapping).
The results of this study were published in the journal Science, and in an university press release highlighting the achievement, MIT assistant professor and co-author Richard Fletcher continued the boiling pot analogy to describe the inherent strangeness of “second sound” in these exotic superfluids.
MIT
Simplified example of “sloshing” heat in a superfluid compared to a normal fluid.
Advertisement - Continue Reading Below
“It’s as if you had a tank of water and made one half nearly boiling,” Fletcher said. “If you then watched, the water itself might look totally calm, but suddenly the other side is hot, and then the other side is hot, and the heat goes back and forth, while the water looks totally still.”
These superfluids are created when a cloud of atoms is subjected to ultra-cold temperatures approaching absolute zero (−459.67 °F). In this rare state, atoms behave differently, as they create an essentially friction-free fluid. It’s in this frictionless state that heat has been theorized to propagate like a wave.
“Second sound is the hallmark of superfluidity, but in ultracold gases so far you could only see it in this faint reflection of the density ripples that go along with it,” lead author Martin Zwierlein said in a press statement. “The character of the heat wave could not be proven before.”
To finally capture this second sound in action, Zweierlein and his team had to think outside the usual thermal box, as there’s a big problem trying to track heat of an ultracold object—it doesn’t emit the usual infrared radiation. So, MIT scientists designed a way to leverage radio frequencies to track certain subatomic particles known as “lithium-6 fermions,” which can be captured via different frequencies in relation to their temperature (i.e. warmer temperatures mean higher frequencies, and vice versa). This novel technique allowed the researchers to essentially zero in on the “hotter” frequencies (which were still very much cold) and track the resulting second wave over time.
This might feel like a big “so what?” After all, when’s the last time you had a close encounter with a superfluid quantum gas? But ask a materials scientist or astronomer, and you’ll get an entirely different answer.
While exotic superfluids may not fill up our lives (yet), understanding the properties of second wave movement could help questions regarding high-temperature superconductors (again, still at very low temperatures) or the messy physics that lie at the heart of neutron stars.
Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.
title: MIT Scientists Capture Heat Waves in Superfluid Quantum Gas
